The user may also enter commands to manage the proof mode (see [Proof mode](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#proofhandling)).

When the proof is complete, use the [`Qed`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Qed) command so the kernel verifies the proof and adds it to the global environment.

Note

1.  Several statements can be simultaneously asserted provided the [`Nested Proofs Allowed`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:flag.Nested-Proofs-Allowed) flag was turned on.

2.  Not only other assertions but any command can be given while in the process of proving a given assertion. In this case, the command is understood as if it would have been given before the statements still to be proved. Nonetheless, this practice is discouraged and may stop working in future versions.

3.  Proofs ended by [`Qed`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Qed) are declared [opaque](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#term-opaque). Their content cannot be unfolded (see [Applying conversion rules](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#applyingconversionrules)), thus realizing some form of *proof-irrelevance*. Proofs that end with [`Defined`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Defined) can be unfolded.

4.  [`Proof`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Proof) is recommended but can currently be omitted. On the opposite side, [`Qed`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Qed) (or [`Defined`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Defined)) is mandatory to validate a proof.

5.  One can also use [`Admitted`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Admitted) in place of [`Qed`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Qed) to turn the current asserted statement into an axiom and exit proof mode.

# Conversion rules

Coq has conversion rules that can be used to determine if two terms are equal by definition in CIC, or [convertible](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#term-convertible). Conversion rules consist of reduction rules and expansion rules. Equality is determined by converting both terms to a normal form, then verifying they are syntactically equal (ignoring differences in the names of bound variables by [alpha-conversion](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#term-alpha-convertible)).

See also

[Applying conversion rules](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#applyingconversionrules), which describes tactics that apply these conversion rules.

Reductions convert terms to something that is incrementally closer to its normal form. For example, [zeta-reduction](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#term-zeta-reduction) removes `let `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)` := `[`term`<sub>`1`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term)` in `[`term`<sub>`2`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term) constructs from a term by replacing [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) with [`term`<sub>`1`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term) wherever [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) appears in [`term`<sub>`2`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term). The resulting term may be longer or shorter than the original.

``` coq
Eval cbv zeta in let i := 1 in i + i.
     = 1 + 1
     : nat
```

Expansions are reductions applied in the opposite direction, for example expanding `2 + 2` to `let i := 2 in i + i`. While applying reductions gives a unique result, the associated expansion may not be unique. For example, `2 + 2` could also be expanded to `let i := 2 in i + 2`. Reductions that have a unique inverse expansion are also referred to as contractions.

The normal form is defined as the result of applying a particular set of conversion rules (beta-, delta-, iota- and zeta-reduction and eta-expansion) repeatedly until it's no longer possible to apply any of them.

Sometimes the result of a reduction tactic will be a simple value, for example reducing `2*3+4` with `cbv beta delta iota` to `10`, which requires applying several reduction rules repeatedly. In other cases, it may yield an expression containing variables, axioms or opaque contants that can't be reduced.

The useful conversion rules are shown below. All of them except for eta-expansion can be applied with conversion tactics such as [`cbv`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.cbv):

> | Conversion name | Description |
> |----|----|
> | beta-reduction | eliminates `fun` |
> | delta-reduction | replaces a defined variable or constant with its definition |
> | zeta-reduction | eliminates `let` |
> | eta-expansion | replaces a term `f` of type `forall a : A, B` with `fun x : A => f x` |
> | match-reduction | eliminates `match` |
> | fix-reduction | replaces a `fix` with a [beta-redex](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#term-beta-redex); recursive calls to the symbol are replaced with the `fix` term |
> | cofix-reduction | replaces a `cofix` with a [beta-redex](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#term-beta-redex); recursive calls to the symbol are replaced with the `cofix` term |
> | iota-reduction | match-, fix- and cofix-reduction together |

[Applying conversion rules](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#applyingconversionrules) describes tactics that only apply conversion rules. (Other tactics may use conversion rules in addition to other changes to the proof state.)

## α-conversion

Two terms are α-convertible if they are syntactically equal ignoring differences in the names of variables bound within the expression. For example `forall x, x + 0 = x` is α-convertible with `forall y, y + 0 = y`.

## β-reduction

β-reduction reduces a beta-redex, which is a term in the form `(fun x => t) u`. (Beta-redex is short for "beta-reducible expression", a term from lambda calculus. See [Beta reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_normal_form#Beta_reduction) for more background.)

Formally, in any [global environment](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#term-global-environment) \\E\\ and [local context](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#term-local-context) \\Γ\\, the beta-reduction rule is:

Beta  
\\\frac{% % }{% E\[Γ\] ⊢ ((λx:T.~t)~u)~\triangleright_β~\subst{t}{x}{u}% }\\

We say that \\\subst{t}{x}{u}\\ is the *β-contraction* of \\((λx:T.~t)~u)\\ and, conversely, that \\((λ x:T.~t)~u)\\ is the *β-expansion* of \\\subst{t}{x}{u}\\.

Terms of the *Calculus of Inductive Constructions* enjoy some fundamental properties such as confluence, strong normalization, subject reduction. These results are theoretically of great importance but we will not detail them here and refer the interested reader to [\[Coq85\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#coq85).

## δ-reduction

δ-reduction replaces variables defined in [local contexts](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#term-local-context) or [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) defined in the [global environment](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#term-global-environment) with their values. Unfolding means to replace a constant by its definition. Formally, this is:

Delta-Local  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% \hspace{3em}% (x:=t:T) ∈ Γ% }{% E\[Γ\] ⊢ x~\triangleright_Δ~t% }\\

<!-- -->

Delta-Global  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% \hspace{3em}% (c:=t:T) ∈ E% }{% E\[Γ\] ⊢ c~\triangleright_δ~t% }\\

[Delta-reduction](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#term-delta-reduction) only unfolds [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) that are marked transparent. Opaque is the opposite of transparent; [delta-reduction](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#term-delta-reduction) doesn't unfold opaque constants.

## ι-reduction

A specific conversion rule is associated with the inductive objects in the global environment. We shall give later on (see Section [Well-formed inductive definitions](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#well-formed-inductive-definitions)) the precise rules but it just says that a destructor applied to an object built from a constructor behaves as expected. This reduction is called ι-reduction and is more precisely studied in [\[PM93a\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#moh93)[\[Wer94\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#wer94).

## ζ-reduction

ζ-reduction removes [let-in definitions](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#let-in) in terms by replacing the defined variable by its value. One way this reduction differs from δ-reduction is that the declaration is removed from the term entirely. Formally, this is:

Zeta  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% \hspace{3em}% \WTEG{u}{U}% \hspace{3em}% \WTE{\Gamma::(x:=u:U)}{t}{T}% }{% E\[Γ\] ⊢ \letin{x}{u:U}{t}~\triangleright_ζ~\subst{t}{x}{u}% }\\

## η-expansion

Another important concept is η-expansion. It is legal to identify any term \\t\\ of functional type \\∀ x:T,~U\\ with its so-called η-expansion

\\λx:T.~(t~x)\\

for \\x\\ an arbitrary variable name fresh in \\t\\.

Note

We deliberately do not define η-reduction:

\\λ x:T.~(t~x)~\not\triangleright_η~t\\

This is because, in general, the type of \\t\\ need not be convertible to the type of \\λ x:T.~(t~x)\\. E.g., if we take \\f\\ such that:

\\f ~:~ ∀ x:\Type(2),~\Type(1)\\

then

\\λ x:\Type(1).~(f~x) ~:~ ∀ x:\Type(1),~\Type(1)\\

We could not allow

\\λ x:\Type(1).~(f~x) ~\triangleright_η~ f\\

because the type of the reduced term \\∀ x:\Type(2),~\Type(1)\\ would not be convertible to the type of the original term \\∀ x:\Type(1),~\Type(1)\\.

## Examples

> Example: Simple delta, fix, beta and match reductions
>
> `+` is a [notation](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/user-extensions/syntax-extensions.html#notations) for `Nat.add`, which is defined with a [`Fixpoint`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Fixpoint).
>
> ``` coq
> Print Nat.add.
> Nat.add =
> fix add (n m : nat) {struct n} : nat :=
>   match n with
>   | 0 => m
>   | S p => S (add p m)
>   end
>      : nat -> nat -> nat
>
> Arguments Nat.add (n m)%nat_scope
> 1 goal
>
>   ============================
>   1 + 1 = 2
> 1 goal
>
>   ============================
>   (fix add (n m : nat) {struct n} : nat :=
>      match n with
>      | 0 => m
>      | S p => S (add p m)
>      end) 1 1 = 2
> 1 goal
>
>   ============================
>   (fun n m : nat =>
>    match n with
>    | 0 => m
>    | S p =>
>        S
>          ((fix add (n0 m0 : nat) {struct n0} : nat :=
>              match n0 with
>              | 0 => m0
>              | S p0 => S (add p0 m0)
>              end) p m)
>    end) 1 1 = 2
> 1 goal
>
>   ============================
>   match 1 with
>   | 0 => 1
>   | S p =>
>       S
>         ((fix add (n m : nat) {struct n} : nat :=
>             match n with
>             | 0 => m
>             | S p0 => S (add p0 m)
>             end) p 1)
>   end = 2
> 1 goal
>
>   ============================
>   S
>     ((fix add (n m : nat) {struct n} : nat :=
>         match n with
>         | 0 => m
>         | S p => S (add p m)
>         end) 0 1) = 2
> ```
>
> The term can be fully reduced with `cbv`:
>
> ``` coq
> Goal 1 + 1 = 2.
> 1 goal
>
>   ============================
>   1 + 1 = 2
> 1 goal
>
>   ============================
>   2 = 2
> ```

## Proof Irrelevance

It is legal to identify any two terms whose common type is a strict proposition \\A : \SProp\\. Terms in a strict propositions are therefore called *irrelevant*.

## Convertibility

Let us write \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t \triangleright u\\ for the contextual closure of the relation \\t\\ reduces to \\u\\ in the global environment \\E\\ and local context \\Γ\\ with one of the previous reductions β, δ, ι or ζ.

We say that two terms \\t_1\\ and \\t_2\\ are *βδιζη-convertible*, or simply convertible, or [definitionally equal](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#term-definitional-equality), in the global environment \\E\\ and local context \\Γ\\ iff there exist terms \\u_1\\ and \\u_2\\ such that \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t_1 \triangleright … \triangleright u_1\\ and \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t_2 \triangleright … \triangleright u_2\\ and either \\u_1\\ and \\u_2\\ are identical up to irrelevant subterms, or they are convertible up to η-expansion, i.e. \\u_1\\ is \\λ x:T.~u_1'\\ and \\u_2 x\\ is recursively convertible to \\u_1'\\, or, symmetrically, \\u_2\\ is \\λx:T.~u_2'\\ and \\u_1 x\\ is recursively convertible to \\u_2'\\. We then write \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t_1 =\_{βδιζη} t_2\\.

Apart from this we consider two instances of polymorphic and cumulative (see Chapter [Polymorphic Universes](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/universe-polymorphism.html#polymorphicuniverses)) inductive types (see below) convertible

\\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t~w_1 … w_m =\_{βδιζη} t~w_1' … w_m'\\

if we have subtypings (see below) in both directions, i.e.,

\\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t~w_1 … w_m ≤\_{βδιζη} t~w_1' … w_m'\\

and

\\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t~w_1' … w_m' ≤\_{βδιζη} t~w_1 … w_m.\\

Furthermore, we consider

\\E\[Γ\] ⊢ c~v_1 … v_m =\_{βδιζη} c'~v_1' … v_m'\\

convertible if

\\E\[Γ\] ⊢ v_i =\_{βδιζη} v_i'\\

and we have that \\c\\ and \\c'\\ are the same constructors of different instances of the same inductive types (differing only in universe levels) such that

\\E\[Γ\] ⊢ c~v_1 … v_m : t~w_1 … w_m\\

and

\\E\[Γ\] ⊢ c'~v_1' … v_m' : t'~ w_1' … w_m '\\

and we have

\\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t~w_1 … w_m =\_{βδιζη} t~w_1' … w_m'.\\

The convertibility relation allows introducing a new typing rule which says that two convertible well-formed types have the same inhabitants.

# Typing rules

The underlying formal language of Coq is a Calculus of Inductive Constructions (CIC) whose inference rules are presented in this chapter. The history of this formalism as well as pointers to related work are provided in a separate chapter; see [Early history of Coq](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/history.html#history).

## The terms

The expressions of the CIC are *terms* and all terms have a *type*. There are types for functions (or programs), there are atomic types (especially datatypes)... but also types for proofs and types for the types themselves. Especially, any object handled in the formalism must belong to a type. For instance, universal quantification is relative to a type and takes the form “*for all x of type* \\T\\, \\P\\”. The expression “\\x\\ *of type* \\T\\” is written “\\x:T\\”. Informally, “\\x:T\\” can be thought as “\\x\\ *belongs to* \\T\\”.

Terms are built from sorts, variables, constants, abstractions, applications, local definitions, and products. From a syntactic point of view, types cannot be distinguished from terms, except that they cannot start by an abstraction or a constructor. More precisely the language of the *Calculus of Inductive Constructions* is built from the following rules.

1.  the sorts \\\SProp\\, \\\Prop\\, \\\Set\\, \\\Type(i)\\ are terms.

2.  variables, hereafter ranged over by letters \\x\\, \\y\\, etc., are terms

3.  constants, hereafter ranged over by letters \\c\\, \\d\\, etc., are terms.

4.  if \\x\\ is a variable and \\T\\, \\U\\ are terms then \\∀ x:T,~U\\ (`forall x:T, U` in Coq concrete syntax) is a term. If \\x\\ occurs in \\U\\, \\∀ x:T,~U\\ reads as “for all \\x\\ of type \\T\\, \\U\\”. As \\U\\ depends on \\x\\, one says that \\∀ x:T,~U\\ is a *dependent product*. If \\x\\ does not occur in \\U\\ then \\∀ x:T,~U\\ reads as “if \\T\\ then \\U\\”. A *non-dependent product* can be written: \\T \rightarrow U\\.

5.  if \\x\\ is a variable and \\T\\, \\u\\ are terms then \\λ x:T .~u\\ (`fun x:T => u` in Coq concrete syntax) is a term. This is a notation for the λ-abstraction of λ-calculus [\[Bar81\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#bar81). The term \\λ x:T .~u\\ is a function which maps elements of \\T\\ to the expression \\u\\.

6.  if \\t\\ and \\u\\ are terms then \\(t~u)\\ is a term (`t u` in Coq concrete syntax). The term \\(t~u)\\ reads as “\\t\\ applied to \\u\\”.

7.  if \\x\\ is a variable, and \\t\\, \\T\\ and \\u\\ are terms then \\\letin{x}{t:T}{u}\\ is a term which denotes the term \\u\\ where the variable \\x\\ is locally bound to \\t\\ of type \\T\\. This stands for the common “let-in” construction of functional programs such as ML or Scheme.

**Free variables.** The notion of free variables is defined as usual. In the expressions \\λx:T.~U\\ and \\∀ x:T,~U\\ the occurrences of \\x\\ in \\U\\ are bound.

**Substitution.** The notion of substituting a term \\t\\ to free occurrences of a variable \\x\\ in a term \\u\\ is defined as usual. The resulting term is written \\\subst{u}{x}{t}\\.

**The logical vs programming readings.** The constructions of the CIC can be used to express both logical and programming notions, according to the Curry-Howard correspondence between proofs and programs, and between propositions and types [\[CFC58\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#cur58)[\[How80\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#how80)[\[dB72\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#bru72).

For instance, let us assume that \\\nat\\ is the type of natural numbers with zero element written \\0\\ and that `True` is the always true proposition. Then \\→\\ is used both to denote \\\nat→\nat\\ which is the type of functions from \\\nat\\ to \\\nat\\, to denote True→True which is an implicative proposition, to denote \\\nat →\Prop\\ which is the type of unary predicates over the natural numbers, etc.

Let us assume that `mult` is a function of type \\\nat→\nat→\nat\\ and `eqnat` a predicate of type \\\nat→\nat→ \Prop\\. The λ-abstraction can serve to build “ordinary” functions as in \\λ x:\nat.~(\kw{mult}~x~x)\\ (i.e. `fun x:nat => mult x x` in Coq notation) but may build also predicates over the natural numbers. For instance \\λ x:\nat.~(\kw{eqnat}~x~0)\\ (i.e. `fun x:nat => eqnat x 0` in Coq notation) will represent the predicate of one variable \\x\\ which asserts the equality of \\x\\ with \\0\\. This predicate has type \\\nat → \Prop\\ and it can be applied to any expression of type \\\nat\\, say \\t\\, to give an object \\P~t\\ of type \\\Prop\\, namely a proposition.

Furthermore `forall x:nat, P x` will represent the type of functions which associate with each natural number \\n\\ an object of type \\(P~n)\\ and consequently represent the type of proofs of the formula “\\∀ x.~P(x)\\”.

## Typing rules

As objects of type theory, terms are subjected to *type discipline*. The well typing of a term depends on a local context and a global environment.

**Local context.** A [local context](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#term-local-context) is an ordered list of declarations of *variables*. The declaration of a variable \\x\\ is either an *assumption*, written \\x:T\\ (where \\T\\ is a type) or a *definition*, written \\x:=t:T\\. Local contexts are written in brackets, for example \\\[x:T;~y:=u:U;~z:V\]\\. The variables declared in a local context must be distinct. If \\Γ\\ is a local context that declares \\x\\, we write \\x ∈ Γ\\. Writing \\(x:T) ∈ Γ\\ means there is an assumption or a definition giving the type \\T\\ to \\x\\ in \\Γ\\. If \\Γ\\ defines \\x:=t:T\\, we also write \\(x:=t:T) ∈ Γ\\. For the rest of the chapter, \\Γ::(y:T)\\ denotes the local context \\Γ\\ enriched with the local assumption \\y:T\\. Similarly, \\Γ::(y:=t:T)\\ denotes the local context \\Γ\\ enriched with the [local definition](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#term-context-local-definition) \\(y:=t:T)\\. The notation \\\[\]\\ denotes the empty local context. Writing \\Γ_1 ; Γ_2\\ means concatenation of the local context \\Γ_1\\ and the local context \\Γ_2\\.

**Global environment.** A [global environment](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#term-global-environment) is an ordered list of *declarations*. Global declarations are either *assumptions*, *definitions* or declarations of inductive objects. Inductive objects declare both constructors and inductive or coinductive types (see Section [Theory of inductive definitions](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#inductive-definitions)).

In the global environment, *assumptions* are written as \\(c:T)\\, indicating that \\c\\ is of the type \\T\\. *Definitions* are written as \\c:=t:T\\, indicating that \\c\\ has the value \\t\\ and type \\T\\. We shall call such names [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant). For the rest of the chapter, the \\E;~c:T\\ denotes the global environment \\E\\ enriched with the assumption \\c:T\\. Similarly, \\E;~c:=t:T\\ denotes the global environment \\E\\ enriched with the definition \\(c:=t:T)\\.

The rules for inductive definitions (see Section [Theory of inductive definitions](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#inductive-definitions)) have to be considered as assumption rules in which the following definitions apply: if the name \\c\\ is declared in \\E\\, we write \\c ∈ E\\ and if \\c:T\\ or \\c:=t:T\\ is declared in \\E\\, we write \\(c : T) ∈ E\\.

**Typing rules.** In the following, we define simultaneously two judgments. The first one \\\WTEG{t}{T}\\ means the term \\t\\ is well-typed and has type \\T\\ in the global environment \\E\\ and local context \\Γ\\. The second judgment \\\WFE{Γ}\\ means that the global environment \\E\\ is well-formed and the local context \\Γ\\ is a valid local context in this global environment.

A term \\t\\ is well typed in a global environment \\E\\ iff there exists a local context \\\Gamma\\ and a term \\T\\ such that the judgment \\\WTEG{t}{T}\\ can be derived from the following rules.

W-Empty  
\\\frac{% % }{% \WF{\[\]}{}% }\\

<!-- -->

W-Local-Assum  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{T}{s}% \hspace{3em}% s \in \Sort% \hspace{3em}% x \not\in \Gamma % \cup E% }{% \WFE{\Gamma::(x:T)}% }\\

<!-- -->

W-Local-Def  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{t}{T}% \hspace{3em}% x \not\in \Gamma % \cup E% }{% \WFE{\Gamma::(x:=t:T)}% }\\

<!-- -->

W-Global-Assum  
\\\frac{% \WTE{}{T}{s}% \hspace{3em}% s \in \Sort% \hspace{3em}% c \notin E% }{% \WF{E;~c:T}{}% }\\

<!-- -->

W-Global-Def  
\\\frac{% \WTE{}{t}{T}% \hspace{3em}% c \notin E% }{% \WF{E;~c:=t:T}{}% }\\

<!-- -->

Ax-SProp  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% }{% \WTEG{\SProp}{\Type(1)}% }\\

<!-- -->

Ax-Prop  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% }{% \WTEG{\Prop}{\Type(1)}% }\\

<!-- -->

Ax-Set  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% }{% \WTEG{\Set}{\Type(1)}% }\\

<!-- -->

Ax-Type  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% }{% \WTEG{\Type(i)}{\Type(i+1)}% }\\

<!-- -->

Var  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% \hspace{3em}% (x:T) \in \Gamma\~~\mbox{or}\~~(x:=t:T) \in \Gamma~\mbox{for some \$t\$}% }{% \WTEG{x}{T}% }\\

<!-- -->

Const  
\\\frac{% \WFE{\Gamma}% \hspace{3em}% (c:T) \in E\~~\mbox{or}\~~(c:=t:T) \in E~\mbox{for some \$t\$}% }{% \WTEG{c}{T}% }\\

<!-- -->

Prod-SProp  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{T}{s}% \hspace{3em}% s \in {\Sort}% \hspace{3em}% \WTE{\Gamma::(x:T)}{U}{\SProp}% }{% \WTEG{\forall~x:T,U}{\SProp}% }\\

<!-- -->

Prod-Prop  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{T}{s}% \hspace{3em}% s \in \Sort% \hspace{3em}% \WTE{\Gamma::(x:T)}{U}{\Prop}% }{% \WTEG{∀ x:T,~U}{\Prop}% }\\

<!-- -->

Prod-Set  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{T}{s}% \hspace{3em}% s \in \\\SProp, \Prop, \Set\\% \hspace{3em}% \WTE{\Gamma::(x:T)}{U}{\Set}% }{% \WTEG{∀ x:T,~U}{\Set}% }\\

<!-- -->

Prod-Type  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{T}{s}% \hspace{3em}% s \in \\\SProp, \Type(i)\\% \hspace{3em}% \WTE{\Gamma::(x:T)}{U}{\Type(i)}% }{% \WTEG{∀ x:T,~U}{\Type(i)}% }\\

<!-- -->

Lam  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{∀ x:T,~U}{s}% \hspace{3em}% \WTE{\Gamma::(x:T)}{t}{U}% }{% \WTEG{λ x:T\mto t}{∀ x:T,~U}% }\\

<!-- -->

App  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{t}{∀ x:U,~T}% \hspace{3em}% \WTEG{u}{U}% }{% \WTEG{(t\\ u)}{\subst{T}{x}{u}}% }\\

<!-- -->

Let  
\\\frac{% \WTEG{t}{T}% \hspace{3em}% \WTE{\Gamma::(x:=t:T)}{u}{U}% }{% \WTEG{\letin{x}{t:T}{u}}{\subst{U}{x}{t}}% }\\

Note

**Prod-Prop** and **Prod-Set** typing-rules make sense if we consider the semantic difference between \\\Prop\\ and \\\Set\\:

- All values of a type that has a sort \\\Set\\ are extractable.

- No values of a type that has a sort \\\Prop\\ are extractable.

Note

We may have \\\letin{x}{t:T}{u}\\ well-typed without having \\((λ x:T.~u)~t)\\ well-typed (where \\T\\ is a type of \\t\\). This is because the value \\t\\ associated with \\x\\ may be used in a conversion rule (see Section [Conversion rules](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/conversion.html#conversion-rules)).

## Subtyping rules

At the moment, we did not take into account one rule between universes which says that any term in a universe of index \\i\\ is also a term in the universe of index \\i+1\\ (this is the *cumulativity* rule of CIC). This property extends the equivalence relation of convertibility into a *subtyping* relation inductively defined by:

1.  if \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t =\_{βδιζη} u\\ then \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t ≤\_{βδιζη} u\\,

2.  if \\i ≤ j\\ then \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ \Type(i) ≤\_{βδιζη} \Type(j)\\,

3.  for any \\i\\, \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ \Set ≤\_{βδιζη} \Type(i)\\,

4.  \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ \Prop ≤\_{βδιζη} \Set\\, hence, by transitivity, \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ \Prop ≤\_{βδιζη} \Type(i)\\, for any \\i\\ (note: \\\SProp\\ is not related by cumulativity to any other term)

5.  if \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ T =\_{βδιζη} U\\ and \\E\[Γ::(x:T)\] ⊢ T' ≤\_{βδιζη} U'\\ then \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ ∀x:T,~T′ ≤\_{βδιζη} ∀ x:U,~U′\\.

6.  if \\\ind{p}{Γ_I}{Γ_C}\\ is a universe polymorphic and cumulative (see Chapter [Polymorphic Universes](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/universe-polymorphism.html#polymorphicuniverses)) inductive type (see below) and \\(t : ∀Γ_P ,∀Γ\_{\mathit{Arr}(t)}, S)∈Γ_I\\ and \\(t' : ∀Γ_P' ,∀Γ\_{\mathit{Arr}(t)}', S')∈Γ_I\\ are two different instances of *the same* inductive type (differing only in universe levels) with constructors

    \\\[c_1 : ∀Γ_P ,∀ T\_{1,1} … T\_{1,n_1} ,~t~v\_{1,1} … v\_{1,m} ;~…;~ c_k : ∀Γ_P ,∀ T\_{k,1} … T\_{k,n_k} ,~t~v\_{k,1} … v\_{k,m} \]\\

    and

    \\\[c_1 : ∀Γ_P' ,∀ T\_{1,1}' … T\_{1,n_1}' ,~t'~v\_{1,1}' … v\_{1,m}' ;~…;~ c_k : ∀Γ_P' ,∀ T\_{k,1}' … T\_{k,n_k}' ,~t'~v\_{k,1}' … v\_{k,m}' \]\\

    respectively then

    \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ t~w_1 … w_m ≤\_{βδιζη} t'~w_1' … w_m'\\

    (notice that \\t\\ and \\t'\\ are both fully applied, i.e., they have a sort as a type) if

    \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ w_i =\_{βδιζη} w_i'\\

    for \\1 ≤ i ≤ m\\ and we have

    \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ T\_{i,j} ≤\_{βδιζη} T\_{i,j}'\\

    and

    \\E\[Γ\] ⊢ A_i ≤\_{βδιζη} A_i'\\

    where \\Γ\_{\mathit{Arr}(t)} = \[a_1 : A_1 ;~ … ;~a_l : A_l \]\\ and \\Γ\_{\mathit{Arr}(t)}' = \[a_1 : A_1';~ … ;~a_l : A_l'\]\\.

The conversion rule up to subtyping is now exactly:

Conv  
\\\frac{% E\[Γ\] ⊢ U : s% \hspace{3em}% E\[Γ\] ⊢ t : T% \hspace{3em}% E\[Γ\] ⊢ T ≤\_{βδιζη} U% }{% E\[Γ\] ⊢ t : U% }\\

**Normal form**. A term which cannot be any more reduced is said to be in *normal form*. There are several ways (or strategies) to apply the reduction rules. Among them, we have to mention the *head reduction* which will play an important role (see Chapter [Tactics](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/tactics.html#tactics)). Any term \\t\\ can be written as \\λ x_1 :T_1 .~… λ x_k :T_k .~(t_0~t_1 … t_n )\\ where \\t_0\\ is not an application. We say then that \\t_0\\ is the *head of* \\t\\. If we assume that \\t_0\\ is \\λ x:T.~u_0\\ then one step of β-head reduction of \\t\\ is:

\\λ x_1 :T_1 .~… λ x_k :T_k .~(λ x:T.~u_0~t_1 … t_n ) ~\triangleright~ λ (x_1 :T_1 )…(x_k :T_k ).~(\subst{u_0}{x}{t_1}~t_2 … t_n )\\

Iterating the process of head reduction until the head of the reduced term is no more an abstraction leads to the *β-head normal form* of \\t\\:

\\t \triangleright … \triangleright λ x_1 :T_1 .~…λ x_k :T_k .~(v~u_1 … u_m )\\

where \\v\\ is not an abstraction (nor an application). Note that the head normal form must not be confused with the normal form since some \\u_i\\ can be reducible. Similar notions of head-normal forms involving δ, ι and ζ reductions or any combination of those can also be defined.

## The Calculus of Inductive Constructions with impredicative Set

Coq can be used as a type checker for the Calculus of Inductive Constructions with an impredicative sort \\\Set\\ by using the compiler option `-impredicative-set`. For example, using the ordinary `coqtop` command, the following is rejected,

Example

``` coq
Fail Definition id: Set := forall X:Set,X->X.
The command has indeed failed with message:
The term "forall X : Set, X -> X" has type "Type"
while it is expected to have type "Set"
(universe inconsistency: Cannot enforce Set+1 <= Set).
```

while it will type check, if one uses instead the `coqtop` `-impredicative-set` option..

The major change in the theory concerns the rule for product formation in the sort \\\Set\\, which is extended to a domain in any sort:

ProdImp  
\\\frac{% E\[Γ\] ⊢ T : s% \hspace{3em}% s ∈ \Sort% \hspace{3em}% E\[Γ::(x:T)\] ⊢ U : \Set% }{% E\[Γ\] ⊢ ∀ x:T,~U : \Set% }\\

This extension has consequences on the inductive definitions which are allowed. In the impredicative system, one can build so-called *large inductive definitions* like the example of second-order existential quantifier (`exSet`).

There should be restrictions on the eliminations which can be performed on such definitions. The elimination rules in the impredicative system for sort \\\Set\\ become:

Set1  
\\\frac{% s ∈ \\\Prop, \Set\\% }{% \[I:\Set\|I→ s\]% }\\

<!-- -->

Set2  
\\\frac{% I~\kw{is a small inductive definition}% \hspace{3em}% s ∈ \\\Type(i)\\% }{% \[I:\Set\|I→ s\]% }\\

# Variants and the `match` construct

## Variants

The [`Variant`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:cmd.Variant) command allows defining types by listing the [inhabitants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-inhabitant) of the type. Each inhabitant is specified by a constructor. For instance, Booleans have two constructors: `true` and `false`. Types can include enumerated types from programming languages, such as Booleans, characters or even the degenerate cases of the unit and empty types. Variant types more generally include enumerated types with arguments or even enumerated types with parametric arguments such as option types and sum types. It also includes predicates or type families defined by cases such as the Boolean reflection or equality predicates. Observing the form of the [inhabitants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-inhabitant) of a variant type is done by case analysis using the `match` expression.

When a constructor of a type takes an argument of that same type, the type becomes recursive, in which case it can be either [`Inductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Inductive) or [`CoInductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/coinductive.html#coq:cmd.CoInductive). The keyword [`Variant`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:cmd.Variant) is reserved for non-recursive types. Natural numbers, lists or streams cannot be defined using [`Variant`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:cmd.Variant).

*Command* `Variant ident_decl binder* | binder*? : type? := |? constructor+| decl_notations?`  
Defines a variant type named [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) (in [`ident_decl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-ident_decl)) with the given list of constructors. No induction scheme is generated for this variant, unless the [`Nonrecursive Elimination Schemes`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/reasoning-inductives.html#coq:flag.Nonrecursive-Elimination-Schemes) flag is on.

`| `[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`*?`  
The `|` separates uniform and non uniform parameters. See [`Uniform Inductive Parameters`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:flag.Uniform-Inductive-Parameters).

This command supports the [`universes(polymorphic)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/universe-polymorphism.html#coq:attr.universes(polymorphic)), [`universes(template)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:attr.universes(template)), [`universes(cumulative)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/universe-polymorphism.html#coq:attr.universes(cumulative)), and [`private(matching)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:attr.private(matching)) attributes.

*Error* `The natural th argument of ident must be ident in type.`  

Example

The Booleans, the unit type and the empty type are respectively defined by:

> ``` coq
> Variant bool : Type := true : bool | false : bool.
> ```

The option and sum types are defined by:

> ``` coq
> Variant option (A : Type) : Type := None : option A | Some : A -> option A.
> ```

*Boolean reflection* is a relation reflecting under the form of a Boolean value when a given proposition `P` holds. It can be defined as a two-constructor type family over `bool` parameterized by the proposition `P`:

``` coq
Variant reflect (P : Prop) : bool -> Set :=
| ReflectT : P -> reflect P true
| ReflectF : ~ P -> reflect P false.
```

[Leibniz equality](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#term-Leibniz-equality) is another example of variant type.

Note

The standard library commonly uses [`Inductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Inductive) in place of [`Variant`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:cmd.Variant) even for non-recursive types in order to automatically derive the schemes [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_rect`, [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_ind`, [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_rec` and [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_sind`. (These schemes are also created for [`Variant`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:cmd.Variant) if the [`Nonrecursive Elimination Schemes`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/reasoning-inductives.html#coq:flag.Nonrecursive-Elimination-Schemes) flag is set.)

### Private (matching) inductive types

*Attribute* `private(matching)`  
This [attribute](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-attribute) can be used to forbid the use of the `match` construct on objects of this inductive type outside of the module where it is defined. There is also a legacy syntax using the `Private` prefix (cf. [`legacy_attr`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-legacy_attr)).

The main use case of private (matching) inductive types is to emulate quotient types / higher-order inductive types in projects such as the [HoTT library](https://github.com/HoTT/HoTT).

Reducing definitions from the inductive's module can expose `match` constructs to unification, which may result in invalid proof terms. Errors from such terms are delayed until proof completion (i.e. on the [`Qed`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Qed)). Use [`Validate Proof`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Validate-Proof) to identify which tactic produced the problematic term.

Example

``` coq
Module Foo.
Interactive Module Foo started
my_nat is defined
fun x : my_nat => match x with
                  | my_O => true
                  | my_S _ => false
                  end
     : my_nat -> bool
Module Foo is defined
The command has indeed failed with message:
case analysis on a private type.
```

## Definition by cases: match

Objects of inductive types can be destructured by a case-analysis construction called *pattern matching* expression. A pattern matching expression is used to analyze the structure of an inductive object and to apply specific treatments accordingly.

``` ebnf
term_match               ::=     match case_item + , return term100 ? with | ? eqn * | end
case_item                ::=     term100 as name ? in pattern ?
eqn                      ::=     pattern + , + | => term
pattern                  ::=     pattern10 : term
                         |       pattern10
pattern10                ::=     pattern1 as name
                         |       pattern1 pattern1 *
                         |       @ qualid pattern1 *
pattern1                 ::=     pattern0 % scope_key
                         |       pattern0 % _ scope_key
                         |       pattern0
pattern0                 ::=     qualid
                         |       { | qualid := pattern * | }
                         |       _
                         |       ( pattern + | )
                         |       number
                         |       string
```

Note that the [`pattern`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern)` ::= `[`pattern10`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern10)` : `[`term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term) production is not supported in `match` patterns. Trying to use it will give this error:

*Error* `Casts are not supported in this pattern.`  

This paragraph describes the basic form of pattern matching. See Section [Multiple and nested pattern matching](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/match.html#mult-match) and Chapter [Extended pattern matching](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/match.html#extendedpatternmatching) for the description of the general form. The basic form of pattern matching is characterized by a single [`case_item`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-case_item) expression, an [`eqn`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-eqn) restricted to a single [`pattern`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern) and [`pattern`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern) restricted to the form [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)` `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`*`.

The expression `match `[`term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term)` return `[`term100`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term100)`? with `[`pattern`<sub>`i`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern)` => `[`term`<sub>`i`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term)`+| end` denotes a *pattern matching* over the term [`term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term) (expected to be of an inductive type \\I\\). The [`term`<sub>`i`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term) are the *branches* of the pattern matching expression. Each [`pattern`<sub>`i`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern) has the form [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)` `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) where [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) must denote a constructor. There should be exactly one branch for every constructor of \\I\\.

The `return `[`term100`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term100) clause gives the type returned by the whole match expression. There are several cases. In the *non-dependent* case, all branches have the same type, and the `return `[`term100`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term100) specifies that type. In this case, `return `[`term100`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term100) can usually be omitted as it can be inferred from the type of the branches [1](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#id3).

In the *dependent* case, there are three subcases. In the first subcase, the type in each branch may depend on the exact value being matched in the branch. In this case, the whole pattern matching itself depends on the term being matched. This dependency of the term being matched in the return type is expressed with an [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) clause where [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) is dependent in the return type. For instance, in the following example:

``` coq
Inductive bool : Type := true : bool | false : bool.
```

the branches have respective types "`or (eq bool true true) (eq bool true false)`" and "`or (eq bool false true) (eq bool false false)`" while the whole pattern matching expression has type "`or (eq bool b true) (eq bool b false)`", the identifier `b` being used to represent the dependency.

Note

When the term being matched is a variable, the `as` clause can be omitted and the term being matched can serve itself as binding name in the return type. For instance, the following alternative definition is accepted and has the same meaning as the previous one.

``` coq
Definition bool_case (b:bool) : or (eq bool b true) (eq bool b false) :=
match b return or (eq bool b true) (eq bool b false) with
| true => or_introl (eq bool true true) (eq bool true false) (eq_refl bool true)
| false => or_intror (eq bool false true) (eq bool false false) (eq_refl bool false)
end.
```

The second subcase is only relevant for indexed inductive types such as the equality predicate (see Section [Equality](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/coq-library.html#coq-equality)), the order predicate on natural numbers or the type of lists of a given length (see Section [Matching objects of dependent types](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/match.html#matching-dependent)). In this configuration, the type of each branch can depend on the type dependencies specific to the branch and the whole pattern matching expression has a type determined by the specific dependencies in the type of the term being matched. This dependency of the return type in the indices of the inductive type is expressed with a clause in the form `in `[`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)` _+ `[`pattern`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern)`+`, where

- [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) is the inductive type of the term being matched;

- the holes `_` match the parameters of the inductive type: the return type is not dependent on them.

- each [`pattern`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern) matches the indices of the inductive type: the return type is dependent on them

- in the basic case which we describe below, each [`pattern`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#grammar-token-pattern) is a name [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident); see [Patterns in in](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/match.html#match-in-patterns) for the general case

For instance, in the following example:

``` coq
Definition eq_sym (A:Type) (x y:A) (H:eq A x y) : eq A y x :=
match H in eq _ _ z return eq A z x with
| eq_refl _ _ => eq_refl A x
end.
```

the type of the branch is `eq A x x` because the third argument of `eq` is `x` in the type of the pattern `eq_refl`. On the contrary, the type of the whole pattern matching expression has type `eq A y x` because the third argument of eq is y in the type of H. This dependency of the case analysis in the third argument of `eq` is expressed by the identifier `z` in the return type.

Finally, the third subcase is a combination of the first and second subcase. In particular, it only applies to pattern matching on terms in a type with indices. For this third subcase, both the clauses `as` and `in` are available.

There are specific notations for case analysis on types with one or two constructors: `if … then … else …` and `let (…,…) := … in …` (see Sections [Pattern-matching on boolean values: the if expression](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/match.html#if-then-else) and [Irrefutable patterns: the destructuring let variants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/match.html#irrefutable-patterns)).

[1](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#id2)  
Except if the inductive type is empty in which case there is no equation that can be used to infer the return type.

# Record types

The [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) command defines types similar to records in programming languages. Those types describe tuples whose components, called fields, can be accessed with projections. Records can also be used to describe mathematical structures, such as groups or rings, hence the synonym [`Structure`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Structure).

## Defining record types

*Command* `RecordStructure record_definition`  
``` ebnf
record_definition        ::=     > ? ident_decl binder * : sort ? := ident ? { record_field * ; ; ? } as ident ? ?
record_field             ::=     #[ attribute + , ] * name field_spec ? | natural ?
field_spec               ::=     binder * of_type_inst
                         |       binder * := term
                         |       binder * of_type_inst := term
of_type_inst             ::=     :  :>  ::  ::> type
```

Defines a non-recursive record type, creating projections for each field that has a name other than `_`. The field body and type can depend on previous fields, so the order of fields in the definition may matter.

Use the [`Inductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Inductive) and [`CoInductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/coinductive.html#coq:cmd.CoInductive) commands to define recursive (inductive or coinductive) records. These commands also permit defining mutually recursive records provided that all of the types in the block are records. These commands automatically generate induction schemes. Enable the [`Nonrecursive Elimination Schemes`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/reasoning-inductives.html#coq:flag.Nonrecursive-Elimination-Schemes) flag to enable automatic generation of elimination schemes for [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record). See [Generation of induction principles with Scheme](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/reasoning-inductives.html#proofschemes-induction-principles).

The [`Class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Class) command can be used to define records that are also [Typeclasses](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#typeclasses), which permit Coq to automatically infer the inhabitants of the record.

`>?`  
If specified, the constructor is declared as a coercion from the class of the last field type to the record name. See [Implicit Coercions](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coercions).

[`ident_decl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-ident_decl)  
The [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) within is the record name.

[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`*`  
[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)s may be used to declare the [inductive parameters](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#term-inductive-parameter) of the record.

`: `[`sort`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/sorts.html#grammar-token-sort)  
The sort the record belongs to. The default is `Type`.

`:= `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`?`  
[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) is the name of the record constructor. If omitted, the name defaults to `Build_`[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) where [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) is the record name.

`as `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`?`  
Specifies the name used to refer to the argument corresponding to the record in the type of projections. If not specified, the name is the first letter of the record name converted to lowercase (see [example](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#record-as-clause)). In constrast, [`Class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Class) command uses the record name as the default (see [example](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#class-arg-name)).

In [`record_field`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-record_field):

> [`attribute`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-attribute), if specified, can only be [`canonical`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/canonical.html#coq:attr.canonical).
>
> [`name`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-name) is the field name. Since field names define projections, you can't reuse the same field name in two different records in the same module. This [example](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#reuse-field-name) shows how to reuse the same field name in multiple records.
>
> [`field_spec`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-field_spec) can be omitted only when the type of the field can be inferred from other fields. For example: the type of `n` can be inferred from `npos` in `Record positive := { n; npos : 0 < n }`.
>
> `| `[`natural`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-natural)  
> Specifies the priority of the field. It is only allowed in [`Class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Class) commands.
>
> `:`  
> Specifies the type of the field.
>
> `:>`  
> If specified, the field is declared as a coercion from the record name to the class of the field type. See [Implicit Coercions](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coercions). Note that this currently does something else in [`Class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Class) commands.
>
> `::`  
> If specified, the field is declared a typeclass instance of the class of the field type. See [Typeclasses](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#typeclasses).
>
> `::>`  
> Acts as a combination of `::` and `:>`.
>
> - [`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`+ : `[`of_type_inst`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-of_type_inst) is equivalent to `: forall `[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`+ , `[`of_type_inst`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-of_type_inst)
>
> - [`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`+ := `[`term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term) is equivalent to `:= fun `[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`+ => `[`term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term)
>
> - [`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`+ `[`of_type_inst`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-of_type_inst)` := `[`term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term) is equivalent to `: forall `[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`+ , `[`type`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-type)` := fun `[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`+ => `[`term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term)
>
> `:= `[`term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term), if present, gives the value of the field, which may depend on the fields that appear before it. Since their values are already defined, such fields cannot be specified when constructing a record.

The [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) command supports the [`universes(polymorphic)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/universe-polymorphism.html#coq:attr.universes(polymorphic)), [`universes(template)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:attr.universes(template)), [`universes(cumulative)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/universe-polymorphism.html#coq:attr.universes(cumulative)), [`private(matching)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:attr.private(matching)) and [`projections(primitive)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:attr.projections(primitive)) attributes.

Example: Defining a record

The set of rational numbers may be defined as:

``` coq
Record Rat : Set := mkRat
 { negative : bool
 ; top : nat
 ; bottom : nat
 ; Rat_bottom_nonzero : 0 <> bottom
 ; Rat_irreducible :
     forall x y z:nat, (x * y) = top /\ (x * z) = bottom -> x = 1
 }.
Rat is defined
negative is defined
top is defined
bottom is defined
Rat_bottom_nonzero is defined
Rat_irreducible is defined
```

The `Rat_*` fields depend on `top` and `bottom`. `Rat_bottom_nonzero` is a proof that `bottom` (the denominator) is not zero. `Rat_irreducible` is a proof that the fraction is in lowest terms.

> Example: Reusing a field name in multiple records
>
> ``` coq
> Module A. Record R := { f : nat }. End A.
>
> Check {| A.f := 0 |}.
> {| A.f := 0 |}
>      : A.R
> {| B.f := 0 |}
>      : B.S
> ```

> Example: Using the "as" clause in a record definition
>
> ``` coq
> Record MyRecord := { myfield : nat } as VarName.
> MyRecord is defined
> myfield is defined
> myfield : MyRecord -> nat
>
> myfield is not universe polymorphic
> Arguments myfield VarName
> myfield is transparent
> Expands to: Constant Top.myfield
> myfield
>      : nat
> where
> ?VarName : [ |- MyRecord]
> myfield
>      : nat
> ```

> Example: Argument name for a record type created using [`Class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Class)
>
> Compare to [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) in the previous example:
>
> ``` coq
> Class MyClass := { myfield2 : nat }.
> MyClass is defined
> myfield2 is defined
> myfield2 : MyClass -> nat
>
> myfield2 is not universe polymorphic
> Arguments myfield2 {MyClass}
> myfield2 is transparent
> Expands to: Constant Top.myfield2
> ```
>
> *Error* `Records declared with the keyword Record or Structure cannot be recursive.`  
> The record name [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) appears in the type of its fields, but uses the [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) command. Use the [`Inductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Inductive) or [`CoInductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/coinductive.html#coq:cmd.CoInductive) command instead.
>
> <!-- -->
>
> *Error* `ident already exists`  
> The fieldname [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) is already defined as a global.
>
> <!-- -->
>
> *Warning* `ident1 cannot be defined because the projection ident2 was not defined`  
> The type of the projection [`ident`<sub>`1`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) depends on previous projections which themselves could not be defined.
>
> <!-- -->
>
> *Warning* `ident cannot be defined.`  
> The projection cannot be defined. This message is followed by an explanation of why it's not possible, such as:
>
> 1.  The [body](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-body) of [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) uses an incorrect elimination for [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) (see [`Fixpoint`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Fixpoint) and [Destructors](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#destructors)).
>
> <!-- -->
>
> *Warning* `identfield cannot be defined because it is informative and identrecord is not`  
> The projection for the named field [`ident`<sub>`field`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) can't be defined. For example, `Record R:Prop := { f:nat }` generates the message "f cannot be defined ... and R is not". Records of sort `Prop` must be non-informative (i.e. indistinguishable). Since `nat` has multiple inhabitants, such as `{| f := 0 |}` and `{| f := 1 |}`, the record would be informative and therefore the projection can't be defined.
>
> See also
>
> Coercions and records in section [Classes as Records](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coercions-classes-as-records).
>
> Note
>
> Records exist in two flavors. In the first, a record [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) with parameters [`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`*`, constructor [`ident`<sub>`0`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident), and fields [`name`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-name)` `[`field_spec`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-field_spec)`*` is represented as a variant type with a single constructor: `Variant `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)` `[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`* : `[`sort`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/sorts.html#grammar-token-sort)` := `[`ident`<sub>`0`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)` ( `[`name`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-name)` `[`field_spec`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-field_spec)` )*` and projections are defined by case analysis. In the second implementation, records have primitive projections: see [Primitive Projections](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#primitive-projections).
>
> During the definition of the one-constructor inductive definition, all the errors of inductive definitions, as described in Section [Inductive types](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#gallina-inductive-definitions), may also occur.

## Constructing records

> ``` ebnf
> term_record              ::=     { | field_val * ; ; ? | }
> field_val                ::=     qualid binder * := term
> ```
>
> Instances of record types can be constructed using either *record form* ([`term_record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-term_record), shown here) or *application form* (see [`term_application`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-term_application)) using the constructor. The associated record definition is selected using the provided field names or constructor name, both of which are global.
>
> In the record form, the fields can be given in any order. Fields that can be inferred by unification or by using obligations (see [Program](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/program.html#programs)) may be omitted.
>
> In application form, all fields of the record must be passed, in order, as arguments to the constructor.
>
> Example: Constructing 1/2 as a record
>
> Constructing the rational \\1/2\\ using either the record or application syntax:
>
> ``` coq
> Theorem one_two_irred : forall x y z:nat, x * y = 1 /\ x * z = 2 -> x = 1.
> ```

## Accessing fields (projections)

> ``` ebnf
> term_projection          ::=     term0 .( qualid univ_annot ? arg * )
>                          |       term0 .( @ qualid univ_annot ? term1 * )
> ```
>
> The value of a field can be accessed using *projection form* ([`term_projection`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-term_projection), shown here) or with *application form* (see [`term_application`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-term_application)) using the projection function associated with the field. Don't forget the parentheses for the projection form. Glossing over some syntactic details, the two forms are:
>
> - [`qualid`<sub>`record`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)`.( @? `[`qualid`<sub>`field`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)` `[`arg`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-arg)`*)`   (projection) and
>
> - `@? `[`qualid`<sub>`field`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)` `[`arg`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-arg)`* `[`qualid`<sub>`record`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)   (application)
>
> where the [`arg`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-arg)s are the parameters of the inductive type. If `@` is specified, all implicit arguments must be provided.
>
> In projection form, since the projected object is part of the notation, it is always considered an explicit argument of [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid), even if it is formally declared as implicit (see [Implicit arguments](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#implicitarguments)).
>
> Example: Accessing record fields
>
> ``` coq
> (* projection form *)
>      = 1
>      : nat
>      = 1
>      : nat
> ```
>
> Example: Matching on records
>
> ``` coq
> Eval compute in (
>   match half with
>   | {| negative := false; top := n |} => n
>   | _ => 0
>   end).
>      = 1
>      : nat
> ```
>
> Example: Accessing anonymous record fields with match
>
> ``` coq
> Record T := const { _ : nat }.
>
> Eval compute in gett inst.
>      = 3
>      : nat
> ```

## Settings for printing records

The following settings let you control the display format for record types:

*Flag* `Printing Records`  
When this [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) is on (this is the default), use the record syntax (shown above) as the default display format.

You can override the display format for specified record types by adding entries to these tables:

*Table* `Printing Record qualid`  
This [table](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-table) specifies a set of qualids which are displayed as records. Use the [`Add`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#coq:cmd.Add) and [`Remove`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#coq:cmd.Remove) commands to update the set of qualids.

<!-- -->

*Table* `Printing Constructor qualid`  
This [table](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-table) specifies a set of qualids which are displayed as constructors. Use the [`Add`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#coq:cmd.Add) and [`Remove`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#coq:cmd.Remove) commands to update the set of qualids.

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Printing Projections`  
Activates the projection form (dot notation) for printing projections (off by default).

Example

``` coq
Check top half. (* off: application form *)
top half
     : nat
half.(top)
     : nat
```

## Primitive Projections

Note: the design of primitive projections is still evolving.

When the [`Primitive Projections`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:flag.Primitive-Projections) flag is on or the [`projections(primitive)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:attr.projections(primitive)) attribute is supplied for a [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) definition, its `match` construct is disabled. To eliminate the record type, one must use its defined primitive projections.

For compatibility, the parameters still appear when printing terms even though they are absent in the actual AST manipulated by the kernel. This can be changed by unsetting the [`Printing Primitive Projection Parameters`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:flag.Printing-Primitive-Projection-Parameters) flag.

There are currently two ways to introduce primitive records types:

1.  Through the [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) command, in which case the type has to be non-recursive. The defined type enjoys eta-conversion definitionally, that is the generalized form of surjective pairing for records: `r` `= Build_``R` `(``r``.(``p`\\\_{1}\\`) …` `r``.(``p`\\\_{n}\\`))`. Eta-conversion allows to define dependent elimination for these types as well.

2.  Through the [`Inductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Inductive) and [`CoInductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/coinductive.html#coq:cmd.CoInductive) commands, when the [body](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-body) of the definition is a record declaration of the form `Build_``R` `{` `p`\\\_{1}\\ `:` `t`\\\_{1}\\`; … ;` `p`\\\_{n}\\ `:` `t`\\\_{n}\\ `}`. In this case the types can be recursive and eta-conversion is disallowed. Dependent elimination is not available for such types; you must use non-dependent case analysis for these.

For both cases the [`Primitive Projections`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:flag.Primitive-Projections) [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) must be set or the [`projections(primitive)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:attr.projections(primitive)) [attribute](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-attribute) must be supplied.

*Flag* `Primitive Projections`  
This [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) turns on the use of primitive projections when defining subsequent records (even through the [`Inductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Inductive) and [`CoInductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/coinductive.html#coq:cmd.CoInductive) commands). Primitive projections extend the Calculus of Inductive Constructions with a new binary term constructor `r.(p)` representing a primitive projection `p` applied to a record object `r` (i.e., primitive projections are always applied). Even if the record type has parameters, these do not appear in the internal representation of applications of the projection, considerably reducing the sizes of terms when manipulating parameterized records and type checking time. On the user level, primitive projections can be used as a replacement for the usual defined ones, although there are a few notable differences.

<!-- -->

*Attribute* `projections(primitive= yesno?)`  
This [boolean attribute](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-boolean-attribute) can be used to override the value of the [`Primitive Projections`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:flag.Primitive-Projections) [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) for the record type being defined.

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Printing Primitive Projection Parameters`  
This compatibility [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) (off by default) reconstructs internally omitted parameters at printing time (even though they are absent in the actual AST manipulated by the kernel).

### Reduction

The basic reduction rule of a primitive projection is `p`\\\_{i}\\ `(Build_``R` `t`\\\_{1}\\ … `t`\\\_{n}\\`)` \\{\rightarrow\_{\iota}}\\ `t`\\\_{i}\\. However, to take the δ flag into account, projections can be in two states: folded or unfolded. An unfolded primitive projection application obeys the rule above, while the folded version delta-reduces to the unfolded version. This allows to precisely mimic the usual unfolding rules of [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant). Projections obey the usual `simpl` flags of the [`Arguments`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#coq:cmd.Arguments) command in particular.

Unfolded primitive projections can be built using the compatibility match syntax for primitive records, or by reducing the compatibility constant.

User-written `match` constructs on primitive records are desugared using the unfolded primitive projections and `let` bindings.

Example

``` coq
#[projections(primitive)] Record Sigma A B := sigma { p1 : A; p2 : B p1 }.
Sigma is defined
p1 is defined
p2 is defined
fun x : Sigma nat (fun _ : nat => nat) =>
let x0 := x in let v := p1 _ _ x0 in let p2 := p2 _ _ x0 in v + v
     : Sigma nat (fun _ : nat => nat) -> nat
fun x : Sigma nat (fun x : nat => x = 0) =>
let x0 := x in
let v := p1 _ _ x0 in
let e : v = 0 := p2 _ _ x0 in ex_intro (fun y : nat => y = 0) v e
     : Sigma nat (fun x : nat => x = 0) -> exists y : nat, y = 0
```

Matches which are equivalent to just a projection have adhoc handling to avoid generating useless `let`:

``` coq
Arguments p1 {_ _} _.
fun x : Sigma nat (fun x : nat => x = 0) => p2 _ _ x
     : forall x : Sigma nat (fun x : nat => x = 0), p1 x = 0
```

*Flag* `Printing Unfolded Projection As Match`  
By default this flag is off and unfolded primitive projections are printed the same as folded primitive projections. By setting this flag, unfolded primitive projections are instead printed as let-style matches in the form `let '{| p := p |} := c in p`.

### Compatibility Constants for Projections

To ease compatibility with ordinary record types, each primitive projection is also defined as an ordinary [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) taking parameters and an object of the record type as arguments, and whose [body](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-body) is an application of the unfolded primitive projection of the same name. These constants are used when elaborating partial applications of the projection. One can distinguish them from applications of the primitive projection if the [`Printing Primitive Projection Parameters`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:flag.Printing-Primitive-Projection-Parameters) flag is off: For a primitive projection application, parameters are printed as underscores while for the compatibility projections they are printed as usual. They cannot be distinguished if the record has no parameters.

# Inductive types and recursive functions

The [`Inductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Inductive) command allows defining types by cases on the form of the [inhabitants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-inhabitant) of the type. These constructors can recursively have arguments in the type being defined. In contrast, in types defined by the [`Variant`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:cmd.Variant) command, such recursive references are not permitted. Inductive types include natural numbers, lists and well-founded trees. Inhabitants of inductive types can recursively nest only a finite number of constructors. So, they are well-founded. This distinguishes them from [`CoInductive`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/coinductive.html#coq:cmd.CoInductive) types, such as streams, whose constructors can be infinitely nested. In Coq, [`Variant`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:cmd.Variant) types thus correspond to the common subset of inductive and coinductive types that are non-recursive.

Due to the recursive structure of inductive types, functions on inductive types generally must be defined recursively using the `fix` expression (see [`term_fix`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#grammar-token-term_fix)) or the [`Fixpoint`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:cmd.Fixpoint) command.

## Inductive types

*Command* `Inductive inductive_definition with inductive_definition*`\
*Command* `Inductive record_definition with record_definition*`  
``` ebnf
inductive_definition     ::=     ident cumul_univ_decl ? binder * | binder * ? : type ? := | ? constructor + | decl_notations ?
constructor              ::=     #[ attribute + , ] * ident binder * of_type_inst ?
```

Defines one or more inductive types and its constructors. Coq generates induction principles depending on the universe that the inductive type belongs to.

The induction principles are named [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_rect`, [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_ind`, [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_rec` and [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_sind`, which respectively correspond to on `Type`, `Prop`, `Set` and `SProp`. Their types expresses structural induction/recursion principles over objects of type [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident). The [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_ind` is always generated, whereas [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_rec` and [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_rect` may be impossible to derive (for example, when [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) is a proposition).

`| `[`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`*?`
