> *Warning* `This command is just asserting the names of arguments of qualid. If this is what you want, add ': assert' to silence the warning. If you want to clear implicit arguments, add ': clear implicits'. If you want to clear notation scopes, add ': clear scopes'`  
>
> `clear scopes`  
> clears argument scopes of [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference)
>
> `extra scopes`  
> defines extra argument scopes, to be used in case of coercion to `Funclass` (see [Implicit Coercions](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coercions)) or with a computed type.
>
> `simpl nomatch`  
> prevents performing a simplification step for [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference) that would expose a match construct in the head position. See [Effects of Arguments on unfolding](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#args-effect-on-unfolding).
>
> `simpl never`  
> prevents performing a simplification step for [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference). See [Effects of Arguments on unfolding](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#args-effect-on-unfolding).
>
> `clear bidirectionality hint`  
> removes the bidirectionality hint, the `&`
>
> [`implicits_alt`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#grammar-token-implicits_alt)  
> use to specify alternative implicit argument declarations for functions that can only be applied to a fixed number of arguments (excluding, for instance, functions whose type is polymorphic). For parsing, the longest list of implicit arguments matching the function application is used to select which implicit arguments are inserted. For printing, the alternative with the most implicit arguments is used; the implict arguments will be omitted if [`Printing Implicit`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#coq:flag.Printing-Implicit) is not set. See the example [here](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#example-more-implicits).

Use [`About`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#coq:cmd.About) to view the current implicit arguments setting for a [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference).

Or use the [`Print Implicit`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#coq:cmd.Print-Implicit) command to see the implicit arguments of an object (see [Displaying implicit arguments](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#displaying-implicit-args)).

## Manual declaration of implicit arguments

Example

``` coq
Inductive list (A : Type) : Type :=
| nil : list A
| cons : A -> list A -> list A.
list is defined
list_rect is defined
list_ind is defined
list_rec is defined
list_sind is defined
cons nat 3 (nil nat)
     : list nat
cons 3 nil
     : list nat
map is defined
map is recursively defined (guarded on 4th argument)
length is defined
length is recursively defined (guarded on 2nd argument)
fun l : list (list nat) => map length l
     : list (list nat) -> list nat
```

Example: Multiple alternatives with [`implicits_alt`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#grammar-token-implicits_alt)

``` coq
Arguments map [A B] f l, [A] B f l, A B f l.
fun l : list (list nat) => map length l = map length l
     : list (list nat) -> Prop
```

## Automatic declaration of implicit arguments

> The "`default implicits`" [`args_modifier`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#grammar-token-args_modifier) clause tells Coq to automatically determine the implicit arguments of the object.
>
> Auto-detection is governed by flags specifying whether strict, contextual, or reversible-pattern implicit arguments must be considered or not (see [Controlling strict implicit arguments](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#controlling-strict-implicit-args), [Controlling contextual implicit arguments](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#controlling-contextual-implicit-args), [Controlling reversible-pattern implicit arguments](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#controlling-rev-pattern-implicit-args) and also [Controlling the insertion of implicit arguments not followed by explicit arguments](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#controlling-insertion-implicit-args)).

Example: Default implicits

``` coq
Inductive list (A:Set) : Set :=
| nil : list A
| cons : A -> list A -> list A.
list is defined
list_rect is defined
list_ind is defined
list_rec is defined
list_sind is defined
cons : forall [A : Set], A -> list A -> list A

Argument A is implicit
nil : forall A : Set, list A
nil : forall {A : Set}, list A

Argument A is implicit and maximally inserted
```

The computation of implicit arguments takes account of the unfolding of [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant). For instance, the variable `p` below has type `(Transitivity R)` which is reducible to `forall x,y:U, R x y -> forall z:U, R y z -> R x z`. As the variables `x`, `y` and `z` appear strictly in the [body](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-body) of the type, they are implicit.

``` coq
Parameter X : Type.
X is declared
Relation is defined
Transitivity is defined
R is declared
p is declared
*** [ p : Transitivity R ]

Expanded type for implicit arguments
p : forall [x y : X], R x y -> forall z : X, R y z -> R x z

Arguments p [x y] _ [z] _
p : forall [x y : X], R x y -> forall z : X, R y z -> R x z

Arguments x, y, z are implicit
a is declared
b is declared
c is declared
r1 is declared
r2 is declared
p r1 r2
     : R a c
```

## Renaming implicit arguments

Example: (continued) Renaming implicit arguments

``` coq
Arguments p [s t] _ [u] _: rename.
p r1 (u:=c)
     : R b c -> R a c
p r1 r2
     : R a c
The command has indeed failed with message:
Flag "rename" expected to rename u into w.
```

## Binding arguments to scopes

> The following command declares that the first two arguments of `plus_fct` are interpreted in the [`scope`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/user-extensions/syntax-extensions.html#grammar-token-scope) delimited by the key `F` and the third argument is first interpreted in the scope delimited by the key `R`, then in `F` (when a notation has no interpretation in `R`).
>
> > ``` coq
> > Arguments plus_fct (f1 f2)%_F x%_R%_F.
> > ```
>
> When interpreting a term, if some of the arguments of [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference) are built from a notation, then this notation is interpreted in the scope stack extended by the scopes bound (if any) to this argument. The effect of these scopes is limited to the argument itself. It does not propagate to subterms but the subterms that, after interpretation of the notation, turn to be themselves arguments of a reference are interpreted according to the argument scopes bound to this reference.

Note

In notations, the subterms matching the identifiers of the notations are interpreted in the scope in which the identifiers occurred at the time of the declaration of the notation. Here is an example:

``` coq
Parameter g : bool -> bool.
g is declared
# true #
     : bool
# true #
     : bool
# false #
     : bool
```

## Effects of [`Arguments`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#coq:cmd.Arguments) on unfolding

- `simpl never` indicates that a [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) should never be unfolded by [`cbn`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.cbn) or [`simpl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.simpl):

  Example

  ``` coq
  Arguments minus n m : simpl never.
  ```

  After that command an expression like `(minus (S x) y)` is left untouched by the tactics [`cbn`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.cbn) and [`simpl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.simpl).

- A [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) can be marked to be unfolded only if it's applied to at least the arguments appearing before the `/` in a [`Arguments`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#coq:cmd.Arguments) command.

  Example

  ``` coq
  Definition fcomp A B C f (g : A -> B) (x : A) : C := f (g x).
  fcomp is defined
  ```

  After that command the expression `(f \o g)` is left untouched by [`simpl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.simpl) while `((f \o g) t)` is reduced to `(f (g t))`. The same mechanism can be used to make a [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) volatile, i.e. always unfolded.

  Example

  ``` coq
  Definition volatile := fun x : nat => x.
  volatile is defined
  ```

- A [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) can be marked to be unfolded only if an entire set of arguments evaluates to a constructor. The `!` symbol can be used to mark such arguments.

  Example

  ``` coq
  Arguments minus !n !m.
  ```

  After that command, the expression `(minus (S x) y)` is left untouched by [`simpl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.simpl), while `(minus (S x) (S y))` is reduced to `(minus x y)`.

- `simpl nomatch` indicates that a [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) should not be unfolded if it would expose a `match` construct in the head position. This affects the [`cbn`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.cbn), [`simpl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.simpl) and [`hnf`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.hnf) tactics.

  Example

  ``` coq
  Arguments minus n m : simpl nomatch.
  ```

  In this case, `(minus (S (S x)) (S y))` is simplified to `(minus (S x) y)` even if an extra simplification is possible.

  In detail: the tactic [`simpl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.simpl) first applies βι-reduction. Then, it expands transparent [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) and tries to reduce further using βι-reduction. But, when no ι rule is applied after unfolding then δ-reductions are not applied. For instance trying to use [`simpl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/equality.html#coq:tacn.simpl) on `(plus n O) = n` changes nothing.

## Bidirectionality hints

When type-checking an application, Coq normally does not use information from the context to infer the types of the arguments. It only checks after the fact that the type inferred for the application is coherent with the expected type. Bidirectionality hints make it possible to specify that after type-checking the first arguments of an application, typing information should be propagated from the context to help inferring the types of the remaining arguments.

An [`Arguments`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#coq:cmd.Arguments) command containing [`arg_specs`<sub>`1`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#grammar-token-arg_specs)` & `[`arg_specs`<sub>`2`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#grammar-token-arg_specs) provides bidirectionality hints. It tells the typechecking algorithm, when type checking applications of [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid), to first type check the arguments in [`arg_specs`<sub>`1`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#grammar-token-arg_specs) and then propagate information from the typing context to type check the remaining arguments (in [`arg_specs`<sub>`2`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/arguments-command.html#grammar-token-arg_specs)).

Example: Bidirectionality hints

In a context where a coercion was declared from `bool` to `nat`:

``` coq
Definition b2n (b : bool) := if b then 1 else 0.
```

Coq cannot automatically coerce existential statements over `bool` to statements over `nat`, because the need for inserting a coercion is known only from the expected type of a subterm:

``` coq
Fail Check (ex_intro _ true _ : exists n : nat, n > 0).
The command has indeed failed with message:
The term "ex_intro ?P true ?y" has type "exists y, ?P y"
while it is expected to have type "exists n : nat, n > 0"
(cannot unify "bool" and "nat").
```

However, a suitable bidirectionality hint makes the example work:

``` coq
Arguments ex_intro _ _ & _ _.
ex_intro (fun n : nat => n > 0) true ?g : exists n : nat, n > 0
     : exists n : nat, n > 0
where
?g : [ |- (fun n : nat => n > 0) true]
```

Coq will attempt to produce a term which uses the arguments you provided, but in some cases involving Program mode the arguments after the bidirectionality starts may be replaced by convertible but syntactically different terms.

# Implicit Coercions

Author  
Amokrane Saïbi

## General Presentation

This section describes the inheritance mechanism of Coq. In Coq with inheritance, we are not interested in adding any expressive power to our theory, but only convenience. Given a term, possibly not typable, we are interested in the problem of determining if it can be well typed modulo insertion of appropriate coercions. We allow to write:

> - `f a` where `f:(forall x:A,B)` and `a:A'` when `A'` can be seen in some sense as a subtype of `A`.
>
> - `x:A` when `A` is not a type, but can be seen in a certain sense as a type: set, group, category etc.
>
> - `f a` when `f` is not a function, but can be seen in a certain sense as a function: bijection, functor, any structure morphism etc.

## Coercion Classes

A class with \\n\\ parameters is any defined name with a type `forall (`[`ident`<sub>`1`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)` : `[`type`<sub>`1`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-type)`)..(`[`ident`<sub>`n`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`:`[`type`<sub>`n`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-type)`), `[`sort`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/sorts.html#grammar-token-sort). Thus a class with parameters is considered as a single class and not as a family of classes. An object of a coercion class is any term of type [`coercion_class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#grammar-token-coercion_class)` `[`term`<sub>`1`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term)` .. `[`term`<sub>`n`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-term). In addition to these user-defined classes, we have two built-in classes:

> - `Sortclass`, the class of sorts; its objects are the terms whose type is a sort (e.g. `Prop` or `Type`).
>
> - `Funclass`, the class of functions; its objects are all the terms with a functional type, i.e. of form `forall x:A,B`.

Formally, the syntax of classes is defined as:

> ``` ebnf
> coercion_class           ::=     Funclass
>                          |       Sortclass
>                          |       reference
> ```

Note

Don't confuse coercion classes with typeclasses, which are records with special properties defined with the [`Class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Class) command.

## Coercions

A name `f` can be declared as a coercion between a source user-defined class `C` with \\n\\ parameters and a target class `D` if one of these conditions holds:

> - `D` is a user-defined class, then the type of `f` must have the form `forall (x₁:A₁)..(xₖ:Aₖ)(y:C v₁..vₙ), D u₁..uₘ` where \\m\\ is the number of parameters of `D`.
>
> - `D` is `Funclass`, then the type of `f` must have the form `forall (x₁:A₁)..(xₖ:Aₖ)(y:C v₁..vₙ)(x:A), B`.
>
> - `D` is `Sortclass`, then the type of `f` must have the form `forall (x₁:A₁)..(xₖ:Aₖ)(y:C v₁..vₙ), s` with `s` a sort.

We then write `f : C >-> D`.

When you declare a new coercion (e.g. with [`Coercion`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coq:cmd.Coercion)), new coercion paths with the same classes as existing ones are ignored. Coq will generate a warning when the two paths may be non convertible. When the `x₁..xₖ` are exactly the `v₁..vₙ` (in the same order), the coercion is said to satisfy the uniform inheritance condition. When possible, we recommend using coercions that satisfy this condition. This guarantees that no spurious warning will be generated.

Note

The built-in class `Sortclass` can be used as a source class, but the built-in class `Funclass` cannot.

To coerce an object `t:C t₁..tₙ` of `C` towards `D`, we have to apply the coercion `f` to it; the obtained term `f _.._ t` is then an object of `D`.

## Reversible Coercions

When a term cannot be coerced (directly) to its expected type, Coq tries to use a reversible coercion (see the [`reversible`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coq:attr.reversible) attribute). Intuitively, Coq synthesizes a new term of the right type that can be coerced to the original one. The new term is obtained by reversing the coercion, that is guessing its input given the output.

More precisely, in order to coerce a term `a : A` to type `B`, Coq finds a reversible coercion `f : B >-> A`, then synthesizes some `?x : B` such that `f ?x = a` (typically through [Canonical Structures](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/canonical.html#canonicalstructures) or [Typeclasses](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#typeclasses)) and finally replaces `a` with the value of `?x`.

If Coq doesn't find a reversible coercion `f : B >-> A`, then it looks for a coercion class `C` equipped with an incoming reversible coercion `g : B >-> C` and a coercion `h : A >-> C` (not necessarily reversible), then synthesizes some `?x : B` such that `g ?x = h a`, and finally replaces `a` with the value of `?x`. If there's another class `D` with a coercion from `C` to `D` and incoming coercions from `A` and `B`, Coq tries `C` before `D`. This ordering is well defined only if the coercion graph happens to be a semi lattice. The intuition behind this ordering is that since coercions forget information, `D` has less information that `C`, and hence inferring `?x : B` from `h a : D` would be harder.

See the [example below](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#example-reversible-coercion).

## Identity Coercions

To make coercions work for both a named class and for `Sortclass` or `Funclass`, use the [`Identity Coercion`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coq:cmd.Identity-Coercion) command. There is an example [here](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#example-identity-coercion).

## Inheritance Graph

Coercions form an inheritance graph with classes as nodes. We call *coercion path* an ordered list of coercions between two nodes of the graph. A class `C` is said to be a subclass of `D` if there is a coercion path in the graph from `C` to `D`; we also say that `C` inherits from `D`. Our mechanism supports multiple inheritance since a class may inherit from several classes, contrary to simple inheritance where a class inherits from at most one class. However there must be at most one path between two classes. If this is not the case, only the *oldest* one is valid and the others are ignored. So the order of declaration of coercions is important.

We extend notations for coercions to coercion paths. For instance `[f₁;..;fₖ] : C >-> D` is the coercion path composed by the coercions `f₁..fₖ`. The application of a coercion path to a term consists of the successive application of its coercions.

## Coercion Classes

*Command* `Coercion reference : coercion_class >-> coercion_class?`\
*Command* `Coercion ident_decl def_body`  
The first form declares the construction denoted by [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference) as a coercion between the two given classes. The second form defines [`ident_decl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-ident_decl) just like [`Definition`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#coq:cmd.Definition) [`ident_decl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-ident_decl)` `[`def_body`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#grammar-token-def_body) and then declares [`ident_decl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-ident_decl) as a coercion between it source and its target. Both forms support the [`local`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.local) attribute, which makes the coercion local to the current section.

`: `[`coercion_class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#grammar-token-coercion_class)` >-> `[`coercion_class`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#grammar-token-coercion_class)`?`  
The source and target classes of the coercion. If unspecified, [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference) must already be a coercion, which enables modifying the [`reversible`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coq:attr.reversible) attribute of [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference). See the [example](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#example-reversible-coercion-attribute) below.

*Attribute* `reversible= yesno?`  
This [attribute](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-attribute) allows the coercion to be used as a [reversible coercion](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#term-reversible-coercion). By default coercions are not reversible except for [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) fields specified using `:>`.

*Attribute* `nonuniform`  
Silence the non uniform inheritance warning.

Deprecated since version 8.18: Use the [`warnings`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#coq:attr.warnings) attribute instead with "-uniform-inheritance".

*Error* `qualid not declared.`  
[`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) is not defined globally.

*Error* `qualid is already a coercion.`  
[`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) is already registered as a coercion.

*Error* `Funclass cannot be a source class.`  
Funclass as a source class is currently not supported. This may change in the future.

*Error* `qualid is not a function.`  
[`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) is not a function, so it cannot be used as a coercion.

*Error* `Cannot find the source class of qualid.`  
Coq can not infer a valid source class.

*Error* `Cannot recognize coercion_class as a source class of qualid.`  
The inferred source class of the coercion differs from the one specified.

*Error* `Cannot find the target class`  
The target class of the coercion is not specified and cannot be inferred. Make sure that the target is not a variable.

*Error* `Found target class coercion_class instead of coercion_class`  
The inferred target class of the coercion differs from the one specified.

*Warning* `qualid does not respect the uniform inheritance condition.`  
The [test for ambiguous coercion paths](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#ambiguous-paths) may yield false positives involving the coercion [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid). Use the [`warnings`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#coq:attr.warnings) attribute with "-uniform-inheritance" to silence this warning.

*Warning* `New coercion path ... is ambiguous with existing ...`  
The check for [ambiguous paths](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#ambiguous-paths) failed. The paths for which this check fails are displayed by a warning in the form `[f₁;..;fₙ] : C >-> D`.

The convertibility checking procedure for coercion paths is complete for paths consisting of coercions satisfying the [uniform inheritance condition](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#term-uniform-inheritance-condition), but some coercion paths could be reported as ambiguous even if they are convertible with existing ones when they have coercions that don't satisfy this condition.

*Warning* `... is not definitionally an identity function.`  
If a coercion path has the same source and target class, that is said to be circular. When a new circular coercion path is not convertible with the identity function, it will be reported as ambiguous.

Some objects can be declared as coercions when they are defined. This applies to [assumptions](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#gallina-assumptions) and constructors of [inductive types and record fields](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#gallina-inductive-definitions). Use `:>` instead of `:` before the type of the assumption to do so. See [`of_type`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-of_type).

*Command* `Identity Coercion ident : coercion_classsrc >-> coercion_classdest`  
Checks that [`coercion_class`<sub>`src`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#grammar-token-coercion_class) is a [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) with a [body](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-body) of the form `fun (x₁:T₁)..(xₙ:Tₙ) => `[`coercion_class`<sub>`dest`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#grammar-token-coercion_class)` t₁..tₘ` where `m` is the number of parameters of [`coercion_class`<sub>`dest`</sub>](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#grammar-token-coercion_class). Then we define an identity function with type `forall (x₁:T₁)..(xₙ:Tₙ)(y:C x₁..xₙ),D t₁..tₘ`, and we declare it as an identity coercion between `C` and `D`. See below for an [example](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#example-identity-coercion).

This command supports the [`local`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.local) attribute, which makes the coercion local to the current section.

*Error* `coercion_class must be a transparent constant.`  

*Command* `SubClass ident_decl def_body`  
If [`type`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-type) is a coercion class [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`'` applied to some arguments then [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident) is defined and an identity coercion of name `Id_`[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_`[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`'` is declared. In other words, this is an abbreviation for

`Definition `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)` := `[`type`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-type)`.` `Identity Coercion Id_`[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`_`[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`' : `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)` >-> `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`'`.

This command supports the [`local`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.local) attribute, which makes the coercion local to the current section.

## Displaying Available Coercions

*Command* `Print Classes`  
Print the list of declared coercion classes in the current context.

<!-- -->

*Command* `Print Coercions`  
Print the list of declared coercions in the current context.

<!-- -->

*Command* `Print Graph`  
Print the list of valid coercion paths in the current context.

<!-- -->

*Command* `Print Coercion Paths coercion_class coercion_class`  
Print the list of valid coercion paths between the two given classes.

## Activating the Printing of Coercions

*Flag* `Printing Coercions`  
When on, this [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) forces all the coercions to be printed. By default, coercions are not printed.

<!-- -->

*Table* `Printing Coercion qualid`  
This [table](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-table) specifies a set of qualids for which coercions are always displayed. Use the [`Add`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#coq:cmd.Add) and [`Remove`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#coq:cmd.Remove) commands to update the set of qualids.

## Classes as Records

*Structures with Inheritance* may be defined using the [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) command.

Use `>` before the record name to declare the constructor name as a coercion from the class of the last field type to the record name. See [`record_definition`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-record_definition).

Use `:>` in the field type to declare the field as a coercion from the record name to the class of the field type. For these coercions, the [`reversible`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coq:attr.reversible) attribute defaults to `yes`. See [`of_type`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-of_type).

## Coercions and Sections

The inheritance mechanism is compatible with the section mechanism. The global classes and coercions defined inside a section are redefined after its closing, using their new value and new type. The classes and coercions which are local to the section are simply forgotten. Coercions with a local source class or a local target class are also forgotten.

## Coercions and Modules

The coercions present in a module are activated only when the module is explicitly imported.

## Examples

There are three situations:

Example: Coercion at function application

`f a` is ill-typed where `f:forall x:A,B` and `a:A'`. If there is a coercion path between `A'` and `A`, then `f a` is transformed into `f a'` where `a'` is the result of the application of this coercion path to `a`.

We first give an example of coercion between atomic inductive types

``` coq
Definition bool_in_nat (b:bool) := if b then 0 else 1.
bool_in_nat is defined
bool_in_nat is now a coercion
0 = true
     : Prop
0 = bool_in_nat true
     : Prop
```

Warning

Note that `Check (true = O)` would fail. This is "normal" behavior of coercions. To validate `true=O`, the coercion is searched from `nat` to `bool`. There is none.

We give an example of coercion between classes with parameters.

``` coq
Parameters (C : nat -> Set) (D : nat -> bool -> Set) (E : bool -> Set).
C is declared
D is declared
E is declared
f is declared
f is now a coercion
g is declared
g is now a coercion
c is declared
T is declared
T c
     : nat
T (g 1 true (f 0 c))
     : nat
```

In the case of functional arguments, we use the monotonic rule of sub-typing. To coerce `t : forall x : A, B` towards `forall x : A', B'`, we have to coerce `A'` towards `A` and `B` towards `B'`. An example is given below:

``` coq
Parameters (A B : Set) (h : A -> B).
A is declared
B is declared
h is declared
h is now a coercion
U is declared
t is declared
U (fun x : A => t x)
     : nat
U (fun x : A => g 1 true (f 0 (t (h x))))
     : nat
```

Remark the changes in the result following the modification of the previous example.

``` coq
Parameter U' : (C 0 -> B) -> nat.
U' is declared
t' is declared
U' (fun x : C 0 => t' x)
     : nat
U' (fun x : C 0 => h (t' (g 1 true (f 0 x))))
     : nat
```

Example: Coercion to a type

An assumption `x:A` when `A` is not a type, is ill-typed. It is replaced by `x:A'` where `A'` is the result of the application to `A` of the coercion path between the class of `A` and `Sortclass` if it exists. This case occurs in the abstraction `fun x:A => t`, universal quantification `forall x:A,B`, global variables and parameters of (co)inductive definitions and functions. In `forall x:A,B`, such a coercion path may also be applied to `B` if necessary.

``` coq
Parameter Graph : Type.
Graph is declared
Node is declared
Node is now a coercion
G is declared
Arrows is declared
Arrows
     : G -> G -> Type
fg is declared
fg
     : G -> G
fg
     : Node G -> Node G
```

Example: Coercion to a function

`f a` is ill-typed because `f:A` is not a function. The term `f` is replaced by the term obtained by applying to `f` the coercion path between `A` and `Funclass` if it exists.

``` coq
Parameter bij : Set -> Set -> Set.
bij is declared
ap is declared
ap is now a coercion
b is declared
b 0
     : nat
ap nat nat b 0
     : nat
```

Example: Reversible coercions

Notice the `:>` on `ssort` making it a [reversible coercion](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#term-reversible-coercion).

``` coq
Structure S := {
  ssort :> Type;
  sstuff : ssort;
}.

Check test (nat : Type).
test (nat : Type)
     : nat
```

Example: Reversible coercions using the [`reversible`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coq:attr.reversible) attribute

Notice there is no `:>` on `ssort'` and the added [`Coercion`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coq:cmd.Coercion) compared to the previous example.

``` coq
Structure S' := {
  ssort' : Type;
  sstuff' : ssort';
}.
```

Since there's no `:>` on the definition of `ssort'`, the [`reversible`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coq:attr.reversible) attribute is not set:

``` coq
Fail Check test' (nat : Type).
The command has indeed failed with message:
The term "nat : Type" has type "Type" while it is expected to have type "S'".
```

The attribute can be set after declaring the coercion:

``` coq
#[reversible] Coercion ssort'.
test' (nat : Type)
     : nat
```

Example: Identity coercions.

``` coq
Definition fct := nat -> nat.

Fail Coercion fct_of_incr_fct : incr_fct >-> Funclass.
The command has indeed failed with message:
Found target class Funclass instead of fct.

Coercion fct_of_incr_fct : incr_fct >-> fct.

Check f' : fct.
f' : fct
     : fct
The command has indeed failed with message:
Illegal application (Non-functional construction):
The expression "f'" of type "incr_fct"
cannot be applied to the term
 "0" : "nat"
f' 0
     : nat
```

Example: Inheritance Graph

Let us see the resulting graph after all these examples.

``` coq
Print Graph.
[h] : A >-> B
[f] : C >-> D
[f; g] : C >-> E
[g] : D >-> E
[Node] : Graph >-> Sortclass
[reverse_coercion] : ReverseCoercionSource >-> ReverseCoercionTarget
[ap] : bij >-> Funclass
[Id_fct_Funclass] : fct >-> Funclass (reversible)
[fct_of_incr_fct; Id_fct_Funclass] : incr_fct >-> Funclass
[fct_of_incr_fct] : incr_fct >-> fct
[ssort] : S >-> Sortclass (reversible)
[ssort'] : S' >-> Sortclass (reversible)
[bool_in_nat] : bool >-> nat
```

# Typeclasses

Typeclasses are types whose values Coq can automatically infer by using user declared instances. It allows for a form of programmatic proof or term search.

This chapter presents a quick reference of the commands related to typeclasses. Additional helpful information can be found in the paper introducing typeclasses to Coq [\[SO08\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#sozeau08) and the literature on type classes in Haskell.

## Typeclass and instance declarations

The syntax for typeclasses and instance declarations is the same as the record syntax of Coq:

``` coq
Class classname (p1 : t1) ⋯ (pn : tn) [: sort] := { f1 : u1 ; ⋯ ; fm : um }.

Instance instancename q1 ⋯ qm : classname p1 ⋯ pn := { f1 := t1 ; ⋯ ; fm := tm }.
```

The `pi : ti` variables are called the *parameters* of the typeclass and the `fi : ti` are called the *methods*. Each typeclass definition gives rise to a corresponding record declaration and each instance is a regular definition whose name is given by `instancename` and type is an instantiation of the record type.

We’ll use the following example typeclass in the rest of the chapter:

``` coq
Class EqDec (A : Type) :=
  { eqb : A -> A -> bool ;
    eqb_leibniz : forall x y, eqb x y = true -> x = y }.
```

This typeclass implements a boolean equality test which is compatible with Leibniz equality on some type. An example implementation is:

``` coq
Instance unit_EqDec : EqDec unit :=
  { eqb x y := true ;
    eqb_leibniz x y H :=
      match x, y return x = y with
      | tt, tt => eq_refl tt
      end }.
```

Using the [`refine`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:attr.refine) attribute, if the term is not sufficient to finish the definition (e.g. due to a missing field or non-inferable hole) it must be finished in proof mode. If it is sufficient a trivial proof mode with no open goals is started.

``` coq
#[refine] Instance unit_EqDec' : EqDec unit := { eqb x y := true }.
```

Note that if you finish the proof with [`Qed`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#coq:cmd.Qed) the entire instance will be opaque, including the fields given in the initial term.

Alternatively, in [`Program Mode`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/program.html#coq:flag.Program-Mode) if one does not give all the members in the Instance declaration, Coq generates obligations for the remaining fields, e.g.:

``` coq
Require Import Program.Tactics.

Next Obligation.
1 goal

  x, y : bool
  H : (if x then y else negb y) = true
  ============================
  x = y
No more goals.
```

One has to take care that the transparency of every field is determined by the transparency of the [`Instance`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Instance) proof. One can use alternatively the [`program`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/program.html#coq:attr.program) attribute to get richer facilities for dealing with obligations.

## Binding typeclasses

Once a typeclass is declared, one can use it in typeclass binders:

``` coq
Definition neqb {A} {eqa : EqDec A} (x y : A) := negb (eqb x y).
neqb is defined
```

When one calls a typeclass method, a constraint is generated that is satisfied only in contexts where the appropriate instances can be found. In the example above, a constraint `EqDec A` is generated and satisfied by `eqa : EqDec A`. In case no satisfying constraint can be found, an error is raised:

``` coq
Fail Definition neqb' (A : Type) (x y : A) := negb (eqb x y).
The command has indeed failed with message:
The following term contains unresolved implicit arguments:
  (fun (A : Type) (x y : A) => negb (eqb x y))
More precisely:
- ?EqDec: Cannot infer the implicit parameter EqDec of eqb whose type is
  "EqDec A" (no type class instance found) in environment:
  A : Type
  x, y : A
```

The algorithm used to solve constraints is a variant of the [`eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.eauto) tactic that does proof search with a set of lemmas (the instances). It will use local hypotheses as well as declared lemmas in the `typeclass_instances` database. Hence the example can also be written:

``` coq
Definition neqb' A (eqa : EqDec A) (x y : A) := negb (eqb x y).
neqb' is defined
```

However, the generalizing binders should be used instead as they have particular support for typeclasses:

- They automatically set the maximally implicit status for typeclass arguments, making derived functions as easy to use as typeclass methods. In the example above, `A` and `eqa` should be set maximally implicit.

- They support implicit quantification on partially applied typeclasses ([Implicit generalization](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#implicit-generalization)). Any argument not given as part of a typeclass binder will be automatically generalized.

- They also support implicit quantification on [Superclasses](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#superclasses).

Following the previous example, one can write:

``` coq
Generalizable Variables A B C.
neqb_implicit is defined
```

Here `A` is implicitly generalized, and the resulting function is equivalent to the one above.

## Parameterized instances

One can declare parameterized instances as in Haskell simply by giving the constraints as a binding context before the instance, e.g.:

``` coq
Program Instance prod_eqb `(EA : EqDec A, EB : EqDec B) : EqDec (A * B) :=
  { eqb x y := match x, y with
               | (la, ra), (lb, rb) => andb (eqb la lb) (eqb ra rb)
               end }.
```

These instances are used just as well as lemmas in the instance hint database.

## Sections and contexts

To ease developments parameterized by many instances, one can use the [`Context`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/sections.html#coq:cmd.Context) command to introduce the parameters into the [local context](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/writing-proofs/proof-mode.html#term-local-context), which works similarly to the command [`Variable`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#coq:cmd.Variable), except it accepts any binding context as an argument, so variables can be implicit, and [Implicit generalization](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/implicit-arguments.html#implicit-generalization) can be used. For example:

``` coq
Section EqDec_defs.
A is declared
EA is declared

#[ global, program ] Instance option_eqb : EqDec (option A) :=
  { eqb x y := match x, y with
         | Some x, Some y => eqb x y
         | None, None => true
         | _, _ => false
         end }.

End EqDec_defs.
option_eqb : forall {A : Type}, EqDec A -> EqDec (option A)

option_eqb is not universe polymorphic
Arguments option_eqb {A}%type_scope {EA}
option_eqb is transparent
Expands to: Constant Top.option_eqb
```

Here the [`global`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.global) attribute redeclares the instance at the end of the section, once it has been generalized by the context variables it uses.

See also

Section [Sections](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/sections.html#section-mechanism)

## Building hierarchies

### Superclasses

One can also parameterize typeclasses by other typeclasses, generating a hierarchy of typeclasses and superclasses. In the same way, we give the superclasses as a binding context:

``` coq
Class Ord `(E : EqDec A) := { le : A -> A -> bool }.
Ord is defined
le is defined
```

Contrary to Haskell, we have no special syntax for superclasses, but this declaration is equivalent to:

``` coq
Class `(E : EqDec A) => Ord A :=
  { le : A -> A -> bool }.
```

This declaration means that any instance of the `Ord` typeclass must have an instance of `EqDec`. The parameters of the subclass contain at least all the parameters of its superclasses in their order of appearance (here A is the only one). As we have seen, `Ord` is encoded as a record type with two parameters: a type `A` and an `E` of type `EqDec A`. However, one can still use it as if it had a single parameter inside generalizing binders: the generalization of superclasses will be done automatically.

``` coq
Definition le_eqb `{Ord A} (x y : A) := andb (le x y) (le y x).
le_eqb is defined
```

To specify sharing of structures, you may want to explicitly specify the superclasses. You can do this directly in regular binders, and with the `!` modifier before typeclass binders. For example:

``` coq
Definition lt `{eqa : EqDec A, !Ord eqa} (x y : A) := andb (le x y) (neqb x y).
lt is defined
```

The `!` modifier switches how Coq interprets a binder. In particular, it uses the implicit arguments mechanism if available, as shown in the example.

### Substructures

Substructures are components of a typeclass which are themselves instances of a typeclass. They often arise when using typeclasses for logical properties, e.g.:

``` coq
Class Reflexive (A : Type) (R : relation A) :=
  reflexivity : forall x, R x x.
```

This declares singleton typeclasses for reflexive and transitive relations, (see the [singleton class](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#singleton-class) variant for an explanation). These may be used as parts of other typeclasses:

``` coq
Class PreOrder (A : Type) (R : relation A) :=
  { PreOrder_Reflexive :: Reflexive A R ;
    PreOrder_Transitive :: Transitive A R }.
PreOrder is defined
PreOrder_Reflexive is defined
PreOrder_Transitive is defined
```

The syntax `::` indicates that each `PreOrder` can be seen as a `Reflexive` relation. So each time a reflexive relation is needed, a preorder can be used instead. This is very similar to the coercion mechanism of `Structure` declarations. The implementation simply declares each projection as an instance.

One can also declare existing objects or structure projections using the [`Existing Instance`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Existing-Instance) command to achieve the same effect.

## Command summary

*Command* `Class record_definition`\
*Command* `Class ident_decl binder* : sort? := constructor`  
The first form declares a record and makes the record a typeclass with parameters [`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)`*` and the listed record fields.

The second form declares a *singleton* typeclass with a single projection. This singleton typeclass is a so-called *definitional typeclass*, represented simply as a definition `ident binders := term` and whose instances are themselves objects of this type.

Definitional typeclasses are not wrapped inside records, and the trivial projection of an instance of such a typeclass is convertible to the instance itself. This can be useful to make instances of existing objects easily and to reduce proof size by not inserting useless trivial projections. The typeclass [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) itself is declared rigid during resolution so that the typeclass abstraction is maintained.

The `>` in [`record_definition`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-record_definition) currently does nothing. In a future version, it will create coercions as it does when used in [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) commands.

Like any command declaring a record, this command supports the [`universes(polymorphic)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/universe-polymorphism.html#coq:attr.universes(polymorphic)), [`universes(template)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#coq:attr.universes(template)), [`universes(cumulative)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/universe-polymorphism.html#coq:attr.universes(cumulative)) and [`private(matching)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/variants.html#coq:attr.private(matching)) attributes.

Note

Don't confuse typeclasses with "coercion classes", described in `implicit coercions<classes-implicit-coercions>`.

When record syntax is used, this command also supports the [`projections(primitive)`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:attr.projections(primitive)) [attribute](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-attribute).

*Command* `Existing Class qualid`  
Declares a typeclass from a previously declared [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) or inductive definition. No methods or instances are defined.

*Warning* `ident is already declared as a typeclass`  
This command has no effect when used on a typeclass.

> *Warning* `A coercion will be introduced instead of an instance in future versions when using ':>' in 'Class' declarations. Replace ':>' with '::' (or use '#[global] Existing Instance field.' for compatibility with Coq < 8.17).`  
> In future versions, `:>` in the [`record_definition`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-record_definition) or [`constructor`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#grammar-token-constructor) will declare a [coercion](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/implicit-coercions.html#coercions), as it does for other [`Record`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#coq:cmd.Record) commands. To eliminate the warning, use `::` instead.
>
> <!-- -->
>
> *Warning* `Ignored instance declaration for “ident”: “term” is not a class`  
> Using the `::` (or deprecated `:>`) syntax in the [`record_definition`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-record_definition) or [`constructor`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/inductive.html#grammar-token-constructor) with a right-hand-side that is not itself a Class has no effect (apart from emitting this warning).

*Command* `Instance ident_decl binder*? : type hint_info? := { field_val* }:= term?`  
Declares a typeclass instance named [`ident_decl`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-ident_decl) of the typeclass [`type`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-type) with the specified parameters and with fields defined by [`field_val`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/records.html#grammar-token-field_val), where each field must be a declared field of the typeclass.

Adds one or more [`binder`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#grammar-token-binder)s to declare a parameterized instance. [`hint_info`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#grammar-token-hint_info) may be used to specify the hint priority. If the priority is not specified, the default is the number of non-dependent binders of the instance. If [`one_pattern`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#grammar-token-one_pattern) is given, terms matching that pattern will trigger use of the instance. Otherwise, use is triggered based on the conclusion of the type.

This command supports the [`local`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.local), [`global`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.global) and [`export`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.export) locality attributes.

Changed in version 8.18: The default value for instance locality outside sections is now [`export`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.export). It used to be [`global`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.global).

Like [`Definition`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#coq:cmd.Definition), it also supports the [`program`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/program.html#coq:attr.program) attribute to switch the type checking to `Program` (chapter [Program](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/program.html#programs)) and to use the obligation mechanism to manage missing fields.

Finally, it supports the lighter [`refine`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:attr.refine) attribute:

*Attribute* `refine`  
This [attribute](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-attribute) can be used to leave holes or not provide all fields in the definition of an instance and open the tactic mode to fill them. It works exactly as if no [body](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-body) had been given and the [`refine`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/tactics.html#coq:tacn.refine) tactic has been used first.

*Command* `Declare Instance ident_decl binder* : term hint_info?`  
In a [`Module Type`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:cmd.Module-Type), declares that a corresponding concrete instance should exist in any implementation of this [`Module Type`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:cmd.Module-Type). This is similar to the distinction between [`Parameter`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/assumptions.html#coq:cmd.Parameter) vs. [`Definition`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#coq:cmd.Definition), or between [`Declare Module`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:cmd.Declare-Module) and [`Module`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:cmd.Module).

*Command* `Existing Instance qualid hint_info?`\
*Command* `Existing Instances qualid+ | natural?`  
Adds a [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) whose type ends with an applied typeclass to the instance database with an optional priority [`natural`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-natural). It can be used for redeclaring instances at the end of sections, or declaring structure projections as instances. This is equivalent to `Hint Resolve ident : typeclass_instances`, except it registers instances for [`Print Instances`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Print-Instances).

<!-- -->

*Command* `Print Instances reference`  
Shows the list of instances associated with the typeclass [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference).

<!-- -->

*Command* `Print Typeclasses`  
Shows the list of declared typeclasses.

<!-- -->

*Tactic* `typeclasses eauto bfsdfsbest_effort? nat_or_var? with ident+?`  
This proof search tactic uses the resolution engine that is run implicitly during type checking, known as *typeclass search*. This tactic uses a different resolution engine than [`eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.eauto) and [`auto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.auto). The main differences are the following:

- Unlike [`eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.eauto) and [`auto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.auto), the resolution is done entirely in the proof engine, meaning that backtracking is available among dependent subgoals, and shelving goals is supported. `typeclasses eauto` is a multi-goal tactic. It analyses the dependencies between subgoals to avoid backtracking on subgoals that are entirely independent.

- The transparency information of databases is used consistently for all hints declared in them. It is always used when calling the unifier. When considering local hypotheses, we use the transparent state of the first hint database given. Using an empty database (created with [`Create HintDb`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:cmd.Create-HintDb) for example) with unfoldable variables and [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) as the first argument of `typeclasses eauto` hence makes resolution with the local hypotheses use full conversion during unification.

- The mode hints (see [`Hint Mode`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:cmd.Hint-Mode)) associated with a typeclass are taken into account by [`typeclasses eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:tacn.typeclasses-eauto). When a goal does not match any of the declared modes for its head (if any), instead of failing like [`eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.eauto), the goal is suspended and resolution proceeds on the remaining goals. If after one run of resolution, there remain suspended goals, resolution is launched against on them, until it reaches a fixed point when the set of remaining suspended goals does not change. Using `solve [typeclasses eauto]` can be used to ensure that no suspended goals remain.

- When considering local hypotheses, we use the union of all the modes declared in the given databases.

- The tactic may produce more than one success when used in backtracking tactics such as `typeclasses eauto; ...`. See [`ltac-seq`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/ltac.html#coq:tacn.ltac-seq).

- Use the [`Typeclasses eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Typeclasses-eauto) command to customize the behavior of this tactic.

`bfsdfs`  
Specifies whether to use breadth-first search or depth-first search. The default is depth-first search, which can be changed with the [`Typeclasses Iterative Deepening`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:flag.Typeclasses-Iterative-Deepening) flag.

`best_effort`  
If the `best_effort` option is given and resolution fails, `typeclasses eauto` returns the first partial solution in which all remaining subgoals fall into one of these categories:

- Stuck goals: the head of the goal has at least one associated declared mode and the constraint does not match any mode declared for its head. These goals are shelved.

- Mode failures: the head of the constraint has at least one matching declared mode, but the constraint couldn't be solved. These goals are left as subgoals of `typeclasses eauto best_effort`.

During type inference, typeclass resolution always uses the `best_effort` option: in case of failure, it constructs a partial solution for the goals and gives a more informative error message. It can be used the same way in interactive proofs to check which instances/hints are missing for a typeclass resolution to succeed.

[`nat_or_var`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/tactics.html#grammar-token-nat_or_var)  
Specifies the maximum depth of the search.

> Warning
>
> The semantics for the limit [`nat_or_var`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/tactics.html#grammar-token-nat_or_var) are different than for [`auto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.auto). By default, if no limit is given, the search is unbounded. Unlike [`auto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.auto), introduction steps count against the limit, which might result in larger limits being necessary when searching with [`typeclasses eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:tacn.typeclasses-eauto) than with [`auto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:tacn.auto).

`with `[`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident)`+`  
Runs resolution with the specified hint databases. It treats typeclass subgoals the same as other subgoals (no shelving of non-typeclass goals in particular), while allowing shelved goals to remain at any point during search.

When `with` is not specified, [`typeclasses eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:tacn.typeclasses-eauto) uses the `typeclass_instances` database by default (instead of `core`). Dependent subgoals are automatically shelved, and shelved goals can remain after resolution ends (following the behavior of Coq 8.5).

Note

`all:once (typeclasses eauto)` faithfully mimics what happens during typeclass resolution when it is called during refinement/type inference, except that *only* declared typeclass subgoals are considered at the start of resolution during type inference, while `all` can select non-typeclass subgoals as well. It might move to `all:typeclasses eauto` in future versions when the refinement engine will be able to backtrack.

<!-- -->

*Tactic* `autoapply one_term with ident`  
The tactic `autoapply` applies [`one_term`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-one_term) using the transparency information of the hint database [`ident`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-ident), and does *no* typeclass resolution. This can be used in [`Hint Extern`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:cmd.Hint-Extern)’s for typeclass instances (in the hint database `typeclass_instances`) to allow backtracking on the typeclass subgoals created by the lemma application, rather than doing typeclass resolution locally at the hint application time.

### Typeclasses Transparent, Typeclasses Opaque

*Command* `Typeclasses Transparent qualid+`  
Makes [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) transparent during typeclass resolution. A shortcut for [`Hint Transparent`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:cmd.Hint-Transparent) [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)`+ : typeclass_instances`

<!-- -->

*Command* `Typeclasses Opaque qualid+`  
Make [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) opaque for typeclass search. A shortcut for [`Hint Opaque`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:cmd.Hint-Opaque) [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid)`+ : typeclass_instances`.

It is useful when some [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) prevent some unifications and make resolution fail. It is also useful to declare constants which should never be unfolded during proof search, like fixpoints or anything which does not look like an abbreviation. This can additionally speed up proof search as the typeclass map can be indexed by such rigid constants (see [Hint databases](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#hintdatabases)).

By default, all [constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) and local variables are considered transparent. One should take care not to make opaque any constant that is used to abbreviate a type, like:

``` coq
Definition relation A := A -> A -> Prop.
```

New in version 8.15: [`Typeclasses Transparent`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Typeclasses-Transparent) and [`Typeclasses Opaque`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Typeclasses-Opaque) support locality attributes like [`Hint`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proofs/automatic-tactics/auto.html#coq:cmd.Hint-Opaque) commands.

Deprecated since version 8.15: The default value for typeclass transparency hints will change in a future release. Hints added outside of sections without an explicit locality are now deprecated. We recommend using [`export`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.export) where possible.

### Settings

*Flag* `Typeclasses Dependency Order`  
This [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) (off by default) respects the dependency order between subgoals, meaning that subgoals on which other subgoals depend come first, while the non-dependent subgoals were put before the dependent ones previously (Coq 8.5 and below). This can result in quite different performance behaviors of proof search.

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Typeclasses Limit Intros`  
This [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) (on by default) controls the ability to apply hints while avoiding (functional) eta-expansions in the generated proof term. It does so by allowing hints that conclude in a product to apply to a goal with a matching product directly, avoiding an introduction.

Warning

This can be expensive as it requires rebuilding hint clauses dynamically, and does not benefit from the invertibility status of the product introduction rule, resulting in potentially more expensive proof search (i.e. more useless backtracking).

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Typeclass Resolution For Conversion`  
This [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) (on by default) controls the use of typeclass resolution when a unification problem cannot be solved during elaboration/type inference. With this flag on, when a unification fails, typeclass resolution is tried before launching unification once again.

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Typeclasses Strict Resolution`  
Typeclass declarations introduced when this [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) is set have a stricter resolution behavior (the flag is off by default). When looking for unifications of a goal with an instance of this typeclass, we “freeze” all the existentials appearing in the goals, meaning that they are considered rigid during unification and cannot be instantiated.

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Typeclasses Unique Solutions`  
When a typeclass resolution is launched we ensure that it has a single solution or fail. This [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) ensures that the resolution is canonical, but can make proof search much more expensive.

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Typeclasses Unique Instances`  
Typeclass declarations introduced when this [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) is set have a more efficient resolution behavior (the flag is off by default). When a solution to the typeclass goal of this typeclass is found, we never backtrack on it, assuming that it is canonical.

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Typeclasses Iterative Deepening`  
When this [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) is set, the proof search strategy is breadth-first search. Otherwise, the search strategy is depth-first search. The default is off. [`Typeclasses eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Typeclasses-eauto) is another way to set this flag.

<!-- -->

*Option* `Typeclasses Depth natural`  
This [option](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-option) sets the maximum proof search depth. The default is unbounded. [`Typeclasses eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Typeclasses-eauto) is another way to set this option.

<!-- -->

*Flag* `Typeclasses Debug`  
Controls whether typeclass resolution steps are shown during search. Setting this [flag](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-flag) also sets [`Typeclasses Debug Verbosity`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:opt.Typeclasses-Debug-Verbosity) to 1. [`Typeclasses eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:cmd.Typeclasses-eauto) is another way to set this flag.

<!-- -->

*Option* `Typeclasses Debug Verbosity natural`  
Determines how much information is shown for typeclass resolution steps during search. 1 is the default level. 2 shows additional information such as tried tactics and shelving of goals. Setting this [option](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#term-option) to 1 or 2 turns on the [`Typeclasses Debug`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:flag.Typeclasses-Debug) flag; setting this option to 0 turns that flag off.

### Typeclasses eauto

*Command* `Typeclasses eauto := debug? ( bfsdfs )? natural?`  
Allows more global customization of the [`typeclasses eauto`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:tacn.typeclasses-eauto) tactic. The options are:

`debug`  
Sets debug mode. In debug mode, a trace of successfully applied tactics is printed. Debug mode can also be set with [`Typeclasses Debug`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:flag.Typeclasses-Debug).

`bfsdfs`  
Specifies whether to use breadth-first search or depth-first search. The default is depth-first search, which can be changed with the [`Typeclasses Iterative Deepening`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:flag.Typeclasses-Iterative-Deepening) flag.

[`natural`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/basic.html#grammar-token-natural)  
Sets the depth limit for the search. The limit can also be set with [`Typeclasses Depth`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/addendum/type-classes.html#coq:opt.Typeclasses-Depth).

# Canonical Structures

Authors  
Assia Mahboubi and Enrico Tassi

This chapter explains the basics of canonical structures and how they can be used to overload notations and build a hierarchy of algebraic structures. The examples are taken from [\[MT13\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#cswcu). We invite the interested reader to refer to this paper for all the details that are omitted here for brevity. The interested reader shall also find in [\[GZND11\]](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/zebibliography.html#cslessadhoc) a detailed description of another, complementary, use of canonical structures: advanced proof search. This latter papers also presents many techniques one can employ to tune the inference of canonical structures.

> 

## Declaration of canonical structures

A canonical structure is an instance of a record/structure type that can be used to solve unification problems involving a projection applied to an unknown structure instance (an implicit argument) and a value. The complete documentation of canonical structures can be found in [Canonical Structures](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/extensions/canonical.html#canonicalstructures); here only a simple example is given.

*Command* `Canonical Structure? reference`\
*Command* `Canonical Structure? ident_decl def_body`  
The first form of this command declares an existing [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference) as a canonical instance of a structure (a record).

The second form defines a new [constant](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) as if the [`Definition`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#coq:cmd.Definition) command had been used, then declares it as a canonical instance as if the first form had been used on the defined object.

This command supports the [`local`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#coq:attr.local) attribute. When used, the structure is canonical only within the [`Section`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/sections.html#coq:cmd.Section) containing it.

[`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) (in [`reference`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/proof-engine/vernacular-commands.html#grammar-token-reference)) denotes an object `(Build_struct c`<sub>`1`</sub>` … c`<sub>`n`</sub>`)` in the structure `struct` for which the fields are `x`<sub>`1`</sub>`, …, x`<sub>`n`</sub>. Then, each time an equation of the form `(x`<sub>`i`</sub>` _)` `=`\\\_{βδιζ}\\ `c`<sub>`i`</sub> has to be solved during the type checking process, [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) is used as a solution. Otherwise said, [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) is canonically used to extend the field `x`<sub>`i`</sub> into a complete structure built on `c`<sub>`i`</sub> when `c`<sub>`i`</sub> unifies with `(x`<sub>`i`</sub>` _)`.

The following kinds of terms are supported for the fields `c`<sub>`i`</sub> of [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid):

- [Constants](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/definitions.html#term-constant) and section variables of an active section, applied to zero or more arguments.

- [`sort`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/sorts.html#grammar-token-sort)s.

- Literal functions: `fun … => …`.

- Literal, (possibly dependent) function types: `… -> …` and `forall …, …`.

- Variables bound in [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid).

Only the head symbol of an existing instance's field `c`<sub>`i`</sub> is considered when searching for a canonical extension. We call this head symbol the *key* and we say "[`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) *keys* the field `x`<sub>`i`</sub> to `k`" when `c`<sub>`i`</sub>'s head symbol is `k`. Keys are the only piece of information that is used for canonical extension. The keys corresponding to the kinds of terms listed above are:

- For constants and section variables, potentially applied to arguments: the constant or variable itself, disregarding any arguments.

- For sorts: the sort itself.

- For literal functions: skip the abstractions and use the key of the body.

- For literal function types: a disembodied implication key denoted `forall _, _`, disregarding both its domain and codomain.

- For variables bound in [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid): a catch-all key denoted `_`.

This means that, for example, `(some_constant x1)` and `(some_constant (other_constant y1 y2) x2)` are not distinct keys.

Variables bound in [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) match any term for the purpose of canonical extension. This has two major consequences for a field `c`<sub>`i`</sub> keyed to a variable of [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid):

1.  Unless another key—and, thus, instance—matches `c`<sub>`i`</sub>, the instance will always be considered by unification.

2.  `c`<sub>`i`</sub> will be considered overlapping not distinct from any other canonical instance that keys `x`<sub>`i`</sub> to one of its own variables.

A record field `x`<sub>`i`</sub> can only be keyed once to each key. Coq prints a warning when [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) keys `x`<sub>`i`</sub> to a term whose head symbol is already keyed by an existing canonical instance. In this case, Coq will not register that [`qualid`](https://rocq-prover.org/doc/V8.19.0/refman/language/core/modules.html#grammar-token-qualid) as a canonical extension. (The remaining fields of the instance can still be used for canonical extension.)

Canonical structures are particularly useful when mixed with coercions and strict implicit arguments.

Example

Here is an example.

``` coq
Require Import Relations.
Setoid is defined
Carrier is defined
Equal is defined
Prf_equiv is defined
is_law is defined
eq_nat_equiv is declared
nat_setoid is defined
```

Thanks to `nat_setoid` declared as canonical, the implicit arguments `A` and `B` can be synthesized in the next statement.

``` coq
Lemma is_law_S : is_law S.
1 goal

  ============================
  is_law (A:=nat_setoid) (B:=nat_setoid) S
```

Note

If a same field occurs in several canonical structures, then only the structure declared first as canonical is considered.

<!-- -->

*Attribute* `canonical= yesno?`
